title: A Brush With Greatness 10: Beginning Cormac - Old Skin
content:
Welcome to the next edition of Brush With Greatness! I’m keewa, your picaro of pigments - if you’re new here, welcome! In this column, I detail my efforts to become a competitive display painter in detail, going through techniques and step-by-step instructions so you can follow along. Last time I finished the wonderful Kuri; this time I’m going to be tackling Cormac the Druid. This wonderful bust, also from Black Crow Miniatures, was sculpted by Lucas Pina Penichet from artwork by Guillermo Gonzalez. I love how characterful this fellow is, with plenty of textures to play with along the way – skin, fabric, feathers, hair, leaves, wood, snail shells; this guy has it all.

Loading...

I followed a tutorial by Arnau Lazaro to paint the skin, beginning by basecoating all the skin with Vallejo Game Color Lustful Purple. This might seem like a strange choice, but it gives some nice shadows with a different colour cast to the normal orangey brown that is the "default" shadow for skin tones. With everything based in Lustful Purple, I created a mix for the base skin tone by mixing the Lustful Purple with Vallejo Game Color Pale Skin, Tan, and Sunset Orange. The method is a little strange, but by keeping the original Lustful Purple in the mix, it preserves the overall coherency of the skin.

Loading...

With that done, I did something I’d not done before: following Mr Lazaro’s tutorial, I mixed together Pro Acryl Fluorescent Orange and Fluorescent Pink and painted it on the cheeks and nose to create a very strong blush. Once again, following the tutorial, I added some Vallejo Game Color Pale Flesh to the orange and pink fluorescent mix and began to carefully glaze the blush until it looked more natural, but still with a nice warm boost.

I shaded the furrows of his wrinkled brow and under the eye-bags with some pure Lustful Purple mixed with Tan. There was quite a lot of going back and forth with the shade mix and the base tone mix, but it’s really important to accentuate the detail on the craggy face. Since I started painting the skin with the airbrush, it’s essential to add this stuff back; otherwise, the skin in general will look far too smooth and unnatural for an old man with weathered skin. Basecoating the hair and beard is an important step in making sure that the skin looks correct, and it stopped me from wasting time applying skin tones to parts of the model that are not supposed to be skin. I bascoated the beard with Vallejo Game Color Charcoal and applied a first highlight by mixing the Charcoal with some Vallejo Game Color Dead White.  

Loading...

I progressively highlighted the beard, hair, and eyebrows by adding white to the Charcoal.

To get the arms looking as though they fit with the face, I glazed the knuckles and elbows with the same fluo mix I used to liven up the nose and cheeks. I also did my usual trick of painting the eyes with Army Painter Speedpaint Goddess Glow to prepare the sockets for painting. I put a bit of Goddess Glow in the hollows of the cheeks and the sides of the nose as well, to add a touch more contrast. To basecoat the eyeballs, I start with Pro Acryl Warm Grey, which I think is a good starting point for eyes, since real eyes are never actually “white”; I don’t want to start there. I also accentuated the under-eye bags with some of the flesh mix, with a bit more Pale Flesh added. The whole process of painting skin generally involves a lot of back and forth until you find the balance you’re looking for; you can see this clearly in the glazing to blend the skin tones with the fluorescents.

Loading...

Following on from the Warm Grey, I painted the first highlight on the eyes, treating them as globes, painting the spherical surface with Pro Acryl Bright Warm Grey, leaving Warm Grey in the corners. To finish the general shape of the eyeball, I added a little Bold Titanium White to the Bright Warm Grey; remember - eyes are never truly white! I also highlighted the tops of the furrows of his brow with Pale Flesh mixed with a really tiny amount of Lustful Purple. Now he looks sufficiently craggy. Now for the most important part: The windows of the soul. I painted the general shape of the Irises using Vallejo Game Colour Dark Green. This step is perhaps the trickiest part of the whole model; painting the eyes on busts is essentially a freehanding exercise. It’s very important to make sure that the gaze is fixed correctly and the eyes aren’t wonky (unless that’s what you’re going for). To fit the overall mood of the figure, I wanted him to be looking at the little bird perched on his hand, as though receiving some news. To achieve this, I went for a quizzical sideways glance.

Loading...

I painted progressively smaller crescents of lighter greens from the same triad - Vallejo Angel Green, Scorpy Green and Bile Green - in the opposite direction to the light source. Once the iris was nicely painted, I carefully made a pupil with Pro Acryl Coal Black.  In order to sell the illusion of the eye being slightly wet, it needs to have a reflection, which I created by painting a catchlight of Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White on the opposite side to the iris highlights from the previous step. 

Loading...

With a little more glazing with the original flesh mix, that concludes the skin and face of Cormac! I really like this method of painting skin; I feel like it has the right amount of warmth and colour contrast to make it really striking. Next time we’ll tackle his clothes and finishing touches!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: TCG Card Shop Simulator
content:
Look, simulator games are tough. I don’t mean challenging; I mean the simulator genre overall has become so wildly oversaturated, and so filled with parodies of the genre, that it can be tough to trust your money when trying a new one. Yet, the simple promise of TCG Card Shop Simulator immediately enthralled my inner child and the hobby shop owner he may have grown into had he not been tied by the shackles of financial responsibility.

To be blunt, I am not a TCG player. The economy of acquiring ever-rotating cards just isn’t my jam. But, like many millennials, the Pokémon TCG was a foundational part of my childhood (and, presumably, a foundational part of my parents’ monthly budgets). That’s to say, I am the perfect, platonic ideal of the target market for TCG Card Shop Simulator, which focuses on managing a store and reproducing the dopamine hit of opening packs of cards (and even playing the game within the game).

Coolness of concept aside, the big question is this: Does TCG Card Shop Simulator have enough meat on its bones, and do the mechanics have enough depth and variety to stay fresh after the novelty has worn off? In a word, yes.

Started From the Bottom, Now We Here

As one might assume, players start TCG Simulator as a brand-new shop owner looking to turn their business into something great. Things don’t start quite at the bottom; the player gets a small storefront and 10 grand in pocket. That cash goes quickly, though, since owners need at least one shelf and some product to start slinging - not to mention having to account for rent, product delivery fees, etc.

The opening hours, while simple and small in scale, still feel exciting and introduce the game's basic elements, along with presenting a few milestones to hit. After I opened In It to Quinn It, I was directed to a virtual phone with a bunch of apps. It was overwhelming, but that’s why it’s great that things start slow. At first, all I needed to worry about was the DIY app, where I could order basic items like shelves, and a supplier app that let me grab a few boxes of basic booster packs. I set the price just a few cents above market value, flipped the CLOSED sign to OPEN, and a few people trickled in.

The game guided me through a few other tasks, and growth was fairly exponential. The money I earned turned into licenses to sell a few other types of packs, which turned into money to buy storage shelves so I didn’t have to keep product on the floor in the corner of my single room. That snowballed into small physical expansions (just a few square feet at a time), a card singles display/sales area, and eventually an employee to handle refilling the shelves while I worked the counter.

Freedom and Expansion

Fairly quickly, though, the guided objectives run out - I’m talking after an hour or less. Then, the game simply is, and the player is free to progress at whatever speed, and in whichever directions, they like. I’ll admit I would have liked to see a bit more in the way of milestones and objectives beyond that. The player earns XP by making sales, which unlock new product licenses to purchase, but it truly is a sandbox without aim. That isn’t a bad thing, but there might have been a middle ground to find or some log and reward for accomplishing different milestones - growing the store, offering new products, making new high sales, etc.

That said, there’s also something calming about not feeling a need to push on just for the sake of growth. I ended every day by restocking my shelves and storage, and most days I’d drain my account to unlock something cool to sell, buy store decor, or maybe add another play table. Other days, I just enjoyed the cash sitting in my account and progressed to the next day. In this way, TCG Simulator is an extremely easy game. I never felt any financial pressure, because (in a shocking departure from reality), my store was constantly serving a high flow of patrons willing to drop dozens to hundreds of dollars on packs/accessories and hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands on singles. If I spent down, I’d just leave my product as it was for a day and I’d be back up in no time. Keep an eye on when bills are due, and that’s about it.

Whether that’s a pro or a con depends on what a given player wants out of TCG Simulator. If you want a relaxing experience to work through at your own pace, this is a great system. If you want a challenge or a more guided milestone experience, this might not be the simulator for you.

How About the Card Game?

Since TCG Card Shop Simulator centers on a game, is the game itself actually interesting? Here, the phenomenon is called Tetramon, an homage both in name and design to the iconic Pokémon franchise. Beyond just selling the cards, there are a few other ways to interact with the product. First, you can just collect them. There are a few different sets, and cards have a variety of finishes - holographic, special borders, full art, etc. Moreover, players can actually play the game through tournaments in their store. I’ll be honest - this isn’t something I engaged with. I do enjoy digital card games, but I get my fix from fully fleshed-out digital TCGs. I’m here for the shop simulator mechanics, and playing the game - which wasn’t playable for much of the game’s early access run - didn’t tickle my fancy. Fortunately, given the game’s aforementioned freedom of pace and direction, this wasn’t an issue. In fact, it was probably great for my bottom line.

The Nitty Gritty

TCG Simulator gets huge props for making the nitty-gritty of monitoring and playing the market largely optional. As any TCG player knows, the value of individual cards, packs, and other products fluctuates wildly not only month to month, but sometimes day to day. For players who want to maximize profit and take advantage of market trends, an in-game app shows increases and decreases in product value (packs, not individual cards). Those who want to can order stock when the price drops (while still selling it for the same price) or hold it until the value comes back up and sell for even more. Moreover, players can look at the cards in their albums and see how a card’s current market value compares to its price history.

I didn’t personally do any of that. Every few nights I’d peruse my stock to make sure it was roughly in line with market value, but I sold my cards (after getting the most valuable graded) at a price appropriate to that moment. Some may enjoy diving into the data and min/maxing, but to me, the juice just isn’t worth the squeeze. A few more bucks don’t make or break anything, and my store kept growing just fine.

Employee management details matter a little more and, unfortunately, can be frustrating. Employees can be given a primary and secondary task, but there’s no central resource to see all employee tasks at once. While talking with individual employees, it doesn’t list their tasks, and there’s no way to simply remove a task. Employees also inconsistently prioritized the primary task over the secondary one. It’s ultimately not a huge deal, but it’s one of the very few frustrations I had with TCG Card Shop Simulator.

They say you shouldn’t mix business with pleasure, but apparently that doesn’t extend to mixing digital recreations of business with facsimiles of pleasure. Overall, TCG Card Shop Simulator is an addictive “just-one-more-day” experience that overperformed my expectations. It may not look pretty or sound particularly great, but the core loop is fun, and the freedom of action and pace make it an easy way to relax and burn some time.

title: Board games have officially gone mainstream - Codenames is now on Netflix
content:
On Tuesday, Netflix Games launched a brand new videogame for Netflix subscribers, Codenames Party, a digital adaptation of the hit head-scratching board game. It even comes with an exclusive new Party Mode, which allows up to 10 players to simultaneously play the role of the clue setter and the clue guesser - and if you know your Codenames, that's a bit of a head-scratching proposition.

For those unfamiliar with Codenames and wondering how to decipher the screenshot lower downthis page, it's a family friendly party game centered on a grid of words. Players split into teams, and each team nominates one player to be the spy master. The spy masters see a secret map of the word grid that indicates certain words they need to help their teammates to identify.

Spy masters take it in turns giving their teammates one-word clues that will hopefully get them to select the correct words on the grid, and steer them away from the opposing team's words, or worse, the deadly 'Assassin' word that results in an instant game over.

I've described pretty much all of the rules from Codenames in one paragraph, one big reason why it's still one of the best board games for families and holiday get-togethers a decade after it was first released. It's a game that can be played by people young, old, and drunk, and everyone has a chance to participate (if not necessarily contribute). Codenames Party offers a digital version of that classic game mode. It runs on a web browser and on "selected smart TVs", with two to ten players able to join at once using their mobile phones as controllers, just like Jackbox Party Pack games.

Party Mode feels even more like a Jackbox Party Pack game. In this mode players see the same grid of 16 words as usual, but everyone is secretly given a list of eight active words, hidden from the other players. Players concoct a one-word clue to connect as many of those words as possible. The game then sets all of these clues as puzzles for everyone else; you can earn points by identifying active words from other players' clues, and also by setting really good clues that other players do a good job of solving.

When I opened the press release with the information about this game I was prepared to be snarky - see my coverage of BMW and Mattel's in-car Uno system for an example of how dismal digital platform crossovers can be - but this seems like a pretty comfortable fit, and a version of the game that might reach a new audience. If you've got Netflix, try it out, and let us know what you think in the Wargamer Discord community. If you want to learn about the latest in old-fashioned Codenames, check out my colleague Mollie's review of Codenames: Critical Role Adventures.

title: Winnipeg toy store owner had 20,000 Pokemon cards stolen, but she's not giving up
content:
Terri Settle isn't selling Pokémon cards to make a quick buck. Her Winnipeg store, Terri's Trinkets and Toys, only has a small inventory of the popular trading cards. "The cards bring in families, and I enjoy watching the children choose the cards that excite them", she tells me. "I intentionally do not keep any high-value individual cards in the store. I sell the cards at the same price as I did 15 years ago."

That hasn't stopped the store being targeted by thieves. The soaring popularity of Pokémon - and the subsequent soar in its value - has caused a spike in Poké-crimes. The hobby's greediest have stalked trucks via GPS and smashed through store walls to grab what amounts to thousands of dollars in product.

Settle opened her store in 2020 after several years selling toys at local flea markets. "Pokémon cards have always been the most frequently shoplifted item from my store", she explains. There have been two major break-ins in the past six years. "Both times", Settle says, "the largest loss came from Pokémon and other types of cards". "It felt evident that the cards were the target, and the rest of the items were stolen simply because they were available."

After the first theft in 2023, Settle invested in video cameras to try and protect her small stock of Pokémon. "My video cameras face from the restroom wall toward the front of the store", she tells me. "It never occurred to me that someone would come through the outside brick wall."

A second theft on September 8, 2026, saw thieves smash through an outside wall, entering the store through drywall access in the bathroom. "From there, the culprit must have crawled into the store and unplugged both my cameras", Settle says.

Settle had around 20,000 Pokémon cards at the time of the theft, 1,000 of which were holographics. All were stolen, along with thousands of MTG, Yugioh, and sports cards. The thief also took packaged Lego sets, toys, jewelery, and videogames, plus Settle's debit machine, personal laptop, and vacuum cleaner.

She estimates she lost $6,000 in lost revenue - $2,000 of which is just Pokémon cards. "I absolutely believe the theft would not have occurred without the Pokémon cards", she adds.

Settle describes the ordeal as "incredibly frustrating", especially given how little value each individual card actually has. "My initial reaction after the September 8th break-in was that it might be time to close my doors, and retire."

Settle's approach to Pokémon is changing because of the theft, but she's not giving up on the game entirely. That's all because of her community. "I have had many incredibly moving things happen in the weeks following", she says.

Though she originally bought all her own stock, Settle says "many people have reached out to me asking if I would accept donations as a result of the recent media coverage." "I have accepted some donations and it has allowed me to restock my shelves without incurring a great deal of expense."

"I have had a very positive response from the community, with people making first visits to my little toy store", she adds. According to the Facebook page, Terri's Trinkets and Toys had one of its best weeks ever following the theft.

Settle is no longer displaying large boxes of Pokémon cards, and she plans to sell reserve stock in blind bags to "keep the cards on the shelves valued under $100". The reason for this goes beyond just trying to deter thieves.

"I have decided that I still want to see Pokémon cards put happy faces on little children", she says, "so I will continue to have a small selection of low value cards available for them". "My own children (now in their thirties) loved Pokémon cards when they were younger." "I think it is remarkable that Pokémon cards have stayed strong in the market despite many other TCGs going by the wayside."

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Assassin
content:
Like rain on an ol’ tin roof. 

Missiles blotted the sun as they fell around the fleeing Assassin, the humming whine of the old ‘Mech’s myomer howling in Cochran’s ears as he was pelted and battered by successive falling salvos coming in from the Catapult down in the valley. The command couch in the old ‘Mech was cramped and stiff while the air was searingly hot and dessicatingly dry; a set of conditions made all the worse by the raining fire that shook and shuddered the walls around him. Gray-Red rocks and dust zipped past as he poured the speed on, ducking Alley-Cat around a boulder to cut the incoming flight off before the sputtering pop of her jump jets split the air and sent them skywards on roiling plumes of plasma.

She was an old frame, and he knew it better than anyone. A ‘Mech long past her prime in the service of his family, his company, and currently his employers. Unfortunately it seemed someone had told the garrison, and the ground, that as well.

Another flight sailed in, a small one, 5 angry bees popping and swirling from the Merlin’s chest launcher to clip Alley Cat’s left leg, boring a hole through an old patch and directly into the actuator. The ‘Mech, and Cochran with it, came down with a crash as the leg crumpled underneath of it and sent them tumbling through the dirt. 

“You alright, Major?” Hoshi’s voice called out, the woman’s Wolfhound bolting through the miasma of heat and dust, the rest of her lance only a few hundred meters behind.

“Well enough, Lieutenant.” Cochran grumbled back, the grinding squeal of the Assassin's leg actuators punctuating the statement as he shoved the ‘Mech to its feet. “But I could be better.”

“Not wrong, we could be back on New Vandenberg having a beer.” She laughed in return, watching as the ‘Mech jogged to meet her. “But that’s gonna have to wait, now isn’t it?”

“That it is.” The Major’s agreement came, low and annoyed as he flexed his ‘Mech’s left hand. “Let’s get to it and get home already.”

— Major Preston Cochran, Taurian Employed Mercenary Command, The Bull’s Head Mercenary Company Assassin ASN-21 Pilot. Qalzi, Unaffiliated, June 12th 3038.  

—

Howdy ‘Mechwarriors and welcome back to another weekly Mech Overview! This week we’re taking a look at the ‘venerable’- really stretching the definition there -old IS scout and interdictor ‘Mech: The Assassin!

I’ll be honest: I have a generally poor opinion of Assassins as a whole and am largely convinced that the only thing that makes it capable of winning a fight against say a watermelon is the fact that it has guns. Even then I might still give it to the watermelon if it was moving fast enough… or was like a really tough watermelon.

The Assassin is a seemingly constant presence on the field of the IS’ wars, from the periphery to Terra and on out to the early dawn of the Clan’s the Assassin has been there, done that, and gotten its shit pushed in for it somewhere along the way.

When a Marshal sees an Assassin we know that the fight isn’t gonna be hard, it’s just gonna be annoying.

Lyran Commonwealth Assassin. Credit: SRM

Chassis

The Assassin is a 40 ton medium that has exactly one thing in common across all of its many variants: it goes 7/11/7- except for the one that goes 7/11/5 -and they carry a mixed load of guns. Usually some energy weapon in the arm and some LRMs or SRMs in the torso.

This is… well it sure is.

They’ve got variable armor loads but in the end they are still largely just 40 tonners… and usually 40 tonners with ammo in them. Not even new Core ammo rules can save that from a bin popping.

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

ASN-21

He’s a man, not a man with a plan mind you; just a man.

Welcome to the year of our lord 2676. We stand in the showroom of the Maltex Corporation. We are Star League acquisition officers. We are being shown a genuine piece of shit… and enough money to set us up for the rest of our lives.

This model of Assassin is pitched as a few things in its time, amongst the grift and graft, most notably that of a scout, light hunter, and as a replacement for the venerable Stinger and Wasp. Note: we have been shown lies. The data is wrong, the performance statistics are overblown, and the Battle ROMs were probably forged.

So what do we actually have here?

Well, a 40 ton 7/11/7 ‘Mech that packs on a whopping 72 pips of armor, this is 52% of the armor load. This paltry amount of armor is 24 points more than a Wasp 1A’s 48 pips. It’s certainly more durable but IDK that I’d call it that much more durable.

So, what is it protecting?

Well, other than a bad cockpit, shite QC, and a shit load of lies about performance? Well, an LRM-5 with 1 ton of ammo, a Medium Laser, and an SRM 2 with one ton of ammo.

Cool. Great use of this chassis.

How much? 749 BV? Oh, so 19 BV less than 2 Wasp 1As. Also of note for the whole ‘in universe bit’: That’s also around 500,000 C-Bills more expensive than 2 Wasp 1As. Cool… why? Like it’s kinda in the little bastard zone but a little bastard whose long range claim to fame is a possible 5 pointer for under 1K should be like 500 BV and named ‘Stinger 3P’.

Liberty’s Rating: D. It’s… I guess it’d be fine for objectives? At least it’s sub 1K BV but if I wanted a 7/11/7 sub 1K BV normal Medium Laser I’d get a Stinger 6G and it’d at least be an MXPL to boot. Honestly that thing might very well win that fight anyhow.

ASN-23

Hey kids? Wanna see an upgrade package?

Remove the SRM 2, you’ve done this? Very good… make the ML an MPL and give the LRM-5 Artemis. Don’t change the armor, keep the same 10 single heat sinks, and retain the same ability to just pop like a grape from the LRM ammo going off.

What? That’s not that much better,  you say? 740 BV for an MPL and an LRM-5 is still kinda too much, you say? Well…

Yea, yea it is.

I know that not every ‘Mech can be a brow beating world beater that can just go toe to toe with everything for the most optimal exchange of BV ever devised but like… even from an in universe perspective who the fuck went ‘Yea, I think a single LRM-5 and an MPL should be enough’? What design genius at defiant got a call from the Lyran High Com. and did this to answer the contract?

Did he at least get bullied for it? Chastised? Fired???

Who am I kidding, knowing the idiots at Defiance I bet he got a fuckin’ promotion.

Liberty’s Rating: D. Man that sure is the same thing but with a blinky light and a weird computer instead of a solid one and some SRMs.

ASN-30

Somehow being more expensive makes a better Little Bastard?

So, the 30 takes a 21, adds 32 pips of armor, rips all the guns out, and powers it with an LFE loaded up with 10 double heat sinks all mounted to an Endo-Steel frame. So, what does it put in all that extra space it has now?

Easy: an ERML and an LB 5-X with one ton of ammo. This is 925 BV and is peak Little Bastard energy. Load it with cluster shells and use it to crit fish enemies that have gotten their armor hammered open while otherwise being a general nuisance for a while anyhow.

Liberty’s Rating: C. This is better than the last ones at least, and at least it’s got some vaguely real armor on it!

ASN-99

Well that’s a big number jump! I hope it’s a big quality jump too!

I… don’t hate this? It’s got a bit more armor than the 30, 98% of possible load at 128 pips, an XL engine, and an ECM suite to power its stealth armor. Armament wise we’ve got a Light PPC, a pair of SRM 2s, a TAG, and… a sword? Sure, why not. All of this is cooled by a 10 pack of double heat sinks.

With a total heat build, with the Stealth on, of 19 heat and you’ve got a pretty workable heat profile of movement -1. At 1,116 BV it’s not the toughest 40 tonners that’s ever existed but with the stealth on and the LPPC firing it’d be an absolute pain in the ass to put down earning it yet another spot in Little Bastard land… even if it is a bit of an expensive one for its damage output.

Liberty’s Rating: C. Honestly kinda like this: Of note, in the OTP Fronc Reaches book the Reaches are attributed as having these in the RAT… I still don’t have them though, annoyingly.

Star League Defense Force Assassin. Credit: Jack Hunter

ASN-101

The year is 3024, and we’re finding ways to save weight.

The 101 is a 21 that has dropped down to 7/11/5 and packs on a meager 64 pips of armor, 47% coverage. It does this so it can add a trio of small lasers to its loadout… For a somewhat familiar 757 BV.

Cool?

It builds movement heat rippling everything off but just dropping the LRM makes it heat neutral on a run and at least gives it a touch more close range damage… even if it is just a trio of small lasers.

Liberty’s Rating: C-. Extra damage and shit is cool, I guess, though going 7/11/5 isn’t great.

ASN-109

Yea, I guess that’s one way to do an upgrade package for the modern era.

The 109 is a rec-guide variant meaning it matches the art. To do this it carries the armor of a 99 with the overall weapons load of the OG 21… or at least something approximating it.

A Light PPC, an MML 5 with 2 tons of ammo in a CASE II bay, and an improved one shot SRM 2. It has stealth armor which is being powered by an Angel ECM suite. The weapons load has a 1 hit pull of 20 heat if it pops the I-OS SRM 2 off with everything else and the stealth armor on. When that’s already fired then you’ve got a clean heat neutral on the run ‘Mech that fires an MML 5 and an LPPC at something with stealth on every turn. For 1,158 BV this is another entry in the ‘stealth armor is annoying, stop doing shit at me’ category of the Little Bastard zone.

Liberty’s Rating: C+. The versatility of the MML is doing a lot here. Having the ability to pitch in in a skirmish before blitzing on someone with some good crit seek is a longstanding favorite archetype of mine and this one certainly can do that. Of the extant main-line Assassins this is certainly the best of them… but what about named ones?

ASN-30 Alice

Who is Alice? What does she want? Is it my kidneys? I bet it’s my kidneys again.

This is the personal ‘Mech of one ‘Mechwarrior Alice Humterderby, helluva name, of the 24th Lyran Guards. It packs the heaviest armor of any Assassin at 134 pips and does something I really wish a normal one would: it boats medium lasers.

Cooled by 10 double heat sinks the Alice carries a C3 Slave, a Beagle Active Probe, a Guardian ECM suite, and 4 IS ERMLs backed up by a Targeting Computer. Powered by a light engine and fully devoid of any and all explosives this thing makes for one hell of an e-war platform that can cover itself while spotting the enemy force for its C3 integrated lance mates. Tack on the movement profile, light engine, and lack of explosives and you’ve got a surprisingly tough little shit head that can hammer some alright damage into someone and only build movement heat.

At 1,507 BV it’s a bit expensive for its damage output but is still workable enough as a movement asset and a real light hunter… like the Assassin always wanted to be.

Liberty’s Rating: B-. a PSR’s worth of TC’d ERMLs backed up by all the EWAR goodies is a fun time and at a relatively affordable price point it’s a pretty alright light whacker/backstabber. I dig it.

Servitor

That’s an absolutely fucking metal name for a ‘Mech that’s basically just a weirdo Solaris jock’s shitbucket.

This ‘Mech started life as an ASN-99 that shed its stealth armor and ECM suite. The TAG, thoroughly not needed in the land of the Game World, has been removed and its spot filled in by a small laser. The sword has been replaced by a small vibroblade. The rest of the armament is rounded out by a Medium X Pulse Laser, and a pair of Small X-Pulse Lasers.

20 heat generated with everything firing/on for 20 heat dissipation makes for a movement heat ‘Mech that can run around with the vibro blade off at Movement-1 until it gets close enough and decides to get to choppin’.

At 1,019 BV this isn’t too bad and could certainly make for a very fun weirdo skirmisher that tries to get after people and chases light ‘Mechs around for most of the game.

Liberty’s Rating: C+. Solaris ‘Mechs are always so weird, I love them.

Final Thoughts

Man, Assassins sure are… something. They run around, do stuff at you, and then explode terribly, or just like fall over at some point. I wish we got a clan grade one, and maybe a few more of the alluded to succ war refits. I’d take a Medium laser boat, maybe something that leans into a more ‘fast support boat’ role with a bigger launcher, perhaps an SRM carrier weirdo. Some variety from the usual would be very cool.

Until next time! Fair weather, good seas and happy guarantee-you’ll-not-go-hungry-ing!

title: D&D Beyond's new Magus class makes multiclassing overpowered again
content:
I have mixed feelings about D&D Beyond's new Magus class. Thematically, it's pretty disjointed. This is a Gish half-caster that tries to be good at a little bit of what makes each class great. Buffs, debuffs, and damage? Let's do them all. What's a spellcaster's biggest problem? Limited spells - let's give 'em more. What's a martial's biggest problem? No spells - and that's easily solved.

It's tough to explain this class flavor-wise. Their magic is briefly described as a sigil-based, 'mystic' affair that's enhanced by a Magus' esoteric order (read: subclasses). It's even tougher to explain it through class archetypes - the Magus is all over the place. I know one thing for sure, though: this is the one of the best multiclass dips in D&D 5.5e.

I took a look at the Magus' early class abilities, and my first thought was 'surely not'. First, we get Esoteric Eye, a bonus action that targets creatures you can see. Just looking at them gives you advantage on spell attacks against them until the end of your next turn. They also get disadvantage on saving throws against your Magus spells.

You can do this a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier, so it's not infinite. Still, you get one use back on a short rest and restore all of them on a long rest. This is literally the only limitation on it apart from sight. No range. No metacurrencies expended.

That seems like it would be ridiculous on a class that doesn't need its bonus action often. My first thought was Fighter, though they might get less use out of the save disadvantage. Free advantage at level one is still a spicy prize.

Perhaps more enticing to a Fighter is the Magus' spellcasting. A level-one dip gets you access to the Wizard's best damage cantrips, plus a few new (slightly more meh) Magus-specific ones. The level-one spell list has many excellent options: Mage Armor, Chromatic Orb, Jump, Longstrider, and Grease, for example. You might end up ignoring them all, though, because Shield is also a Magus spell. 'Spam Shield' is a top tactic for any martial taking the Magic Initiate feat, and now you don't even need to waste a feat.

The rest of the Magus' spell list is a 'who's who' of the best spells in the game. Misty Step is here, and so is Counterspell. We've got Haste and Dispel Magic. Fireball, Fly, Globe of Invulnerability? The Magus has pinched them all. This isn't as great as it sounds, given how long a Magus has to wait for high-level spell slots. But it tells us a lot about the class' core design philosophy - look at what works for everyone else, and copy that.

We get one more ability at level one, and it's Weapon Mastery. That's a nice addition for any spellcaster that wants to go full Gish by another route.

If you thought we were done with absurd low-level abilities, let me introduce you to level two. We first get a Fighting Style that, alternatively, offers the power to add your Intelligence modifier to concentration saves. If you ever actually lose concentration, you also gain Temporary Hit Points equal to twice the spell's level plus your Intelligence modifier.

Slightly more in the 'what the fuck' department is Mystic Mark. It's a bonus action that lets you choose a levelled spell and, spending a spell slot equal or higher than its level, choose a damage type.

That damage type is one the spell deals, or it can be Force damage. Your two options are 'aegis', which gives you resistance to the chosen damage type, or 'enspel', that lets you replace a weapon or unarmed strike's damage with your chosen type. The bonus action's effects last for one hour, or until you decide to cast the spell you chose at the start of this action.

Let me be clear. At level two, the Magus can give themself the ability to deal Force damage - the rarest damage resistance in the game - for one hour, uninterrupted. All it costs is holding off casting a level-one spell.

Things get a little less interesting from here, but that's mainly because those first two levels overshadow everything else. Level five lets you add your Intelligence modifier to a failed ability check once per rest, because this class wants to be good at everything. It also lets you cast a Magus cantrip for free after attacking, provided you didn't already benefit from an Extra Attack feature (something this class doesn't have - a clear sign it was designed with multiclassing in mind).

Level six lets you regain spell slots with a combined level equal to half your Magus level, once per long rest. If Wizards can have Arcane Recovery, why can't we?

Level nine tweaks your Mystic Mark so, when you cast the spell you were holding, you get the spell slot back. Level 10 offers another bonus action, but this one gives you 60 feet of Truesight for 10 minutes, and using Esoteric Eye in that time doesn't expend its uses. Literally no one is safe.

Level 11 improves Mystic Mark again by offering Temporary HP or an extra 1d6 of attack damage, depending on whether you choose to use aegis or enspel. Level 15 brings Sorcerous Shielding, which gives you any one magic resistance and extra protection from spell saves and spell attacks. By level 18, you can cast one level-six spell without a slot once per day - and doing so actually recovers a level-five-or-lower spell slot.

Our capstone, finally, buffs Strength or Dexterity by 2, and it lets you use that level-six feature twice a day.

There's some interesting stuff going on at higher levels, but my first impression is the Magus is a bit meh at higher tiers - at least, if you play it as a Gish. There's simply not enough focus on improving your martial capabilities. Your constant source of advantage guarantees consistent hits, but without damage increases or abilities like Extra Attack, you're never going to rival a Fighter. Your cantrips are all damage-focused, too, so you can't even enhance your abilities the way an Eldritch Knight or Arcane Archer would.

Plus, you're still MAD, making it tough to juggle your physical abilities. You're basically a Paladin without the smite (though, thanks to all those free spell slots, you can spam a lot more spells).

That half-caster cap on your spell slots makes this less appealing than a full caster for an all-magic build, too. The progression is simply too slow.

A quick little multiclass dip, though? That sounds powerful.

Sure, you miss out on the Magus many, varied subclasses (all of which seem to be copying another class' homework). There's a Magus that offers teleporting abilities that look very easy to break. Another adds healing spells and Defender powers, while the next is all about necromancy. There's a stealthy Rogue/Monk stand-in, plus a divination subclass that literally gives you Portent. The last one asks you to imagine a world where Druids have all the Rogue's dexterous extra bonus actions.

I think the trade off is worth-it though. I want to stress think in the interest of fairness, because I haven't finished all my simulations and whiteboard math-ing just yet. But, on first impression? The Magus looked at D&D 5.5e's lackluster multiclass builds and said 'hold my beer'.

Want to share your own takes on the Magus? I'm always happy to be proved wrong over in the Wargamer Discord. Tell me if I've missed something, I dare you. If you want to swot up beforehand, you can also check out our guide to DnD classes.

title: Games from the Crypt #23 - The A-hole Dracula Paradox
content:
Spooky season is here and as we do down here in the Games Crypt, we exhume another undead tabletop terror, dragging it into the harsh light of this column once again. And this time, it’s one of my very favorite horror-themed board games. It comes from a time when not every Games Workshop title required an additional $500 purchase and their design brief was still somewhere along the lines of “can we play this down the pub after a few pints”. In fact, the author of this game, Stephen Hand, is shown in the original designer photo with a beer. Of course I’m going on about the best game ever made about Dracula, Fury of Dracula. It’s timely too because a brand new 5th edition of the game is on shelves in time for Halloween courtesy Avalon Hill, with some design updates a new “quick play” mode developed by the great Craig Van Ness.

I’ve owned every edition of this great game to date except this one, and I’m probably going to wind up with it at some point. Every copy of the game I’ve had I’ve cherished up until it goes out of print and the eBay price hits a “20% of a new guitar” level. I would fully expect this edition to follow a similar trajectory. There have definitely been some ups and downs in both design and production quality over the almost 40 years it has drifted in and out of print. The second edition, published with much ballyhoo by Fantasy Flight Games in 2005 offered some fairly heavy-handed redevelopment by Kevin Wilson that turned it into very much a FFG-style design. The 3rd and 4th editions course-corrected somewhat but didn’t look as good and still veered from the simplicity and chaos of the original in favor of modern balance. The first edition, in that Games Workshop bookshelf box with the bold-line artwork, magazine paper cards, and garish gothic fonts, remains the best version of the game to date.

At its bloody heart, Fury of Dracula is a jumped-up take on the classic family deduction game Scotland Yard with some more adventure game-style elements such as combat, items, encounters, and events. And the big bad - which is controlled by a player in opposition to everyone else at the table - is Count Dracula instead of the nebulous “Mr. X”. As in that venerable, much-beloved chestnut (which itself as pretty great game), the villain secretly moves around on a hidden map while the other players try to use clues and evidence to triangulate and eventually corner them. And Dracula has some traps and tricks up his immaculately tailored sleeve, stationing dark minions to waylay the hunters.

This all takes place on a lovely map of the population centers, roads, railways, and waterways of Victorian-era Europe as Dr, Seward, Lord Godalming (Arthur Holmwood for those who aren’t Stoker scholars), and of course the inimitable Van Helsing search for Local Rumours, weapons, and signs that the Count has rolled through. I love that the game is a little closer to the pulpy, two-fisted vampire busting of the Hammer Horror films than the stately, epistolary tone of the novel- combat can and does happen and is resolved in one of those vintage Games Workshop rock-paper-scissor mechanics.

There is an element of this game that some have viewed as a flaw. I call it the Asshole Dracula Paradox. An Asshole Dracula can make the game dramatically unfun if they play in such a way that they aren’t taunting and teasing the hunters and they just run away as quickly and as far as they can. An extremely aggressive Dracula player can also make life pretty miserable for the hunters as the minions and abilities at his dark disposal are quite powerful. So it falls on the Dracula player to almost be a kind of antagonistic game master and play with a “fun first” mentality to support the other players’ good time. This kind of creates a paradox in that playing to win as Dracula can make it unpleasant, but without a sense of risk, danger, and opposition the frisson of the game suffers. The simple solution is that the most experienced player plays Dracula because they will understand how to don the cape and fangs most effectively and most interestingly.

And when you have a good Dracula player at the table, this game remains one of my all time favorite gaming experiences. It’s atmospheric, strongly narrative, and it really captures the tone, feel, and themes of the Dracula story. I love how it expands on it as well, turning what is essentially a kind of drawing room drama about a real estate transaction gone horribly wrong into a continent-spanning horror epic full of surprise, close calls, and even closer encounters with the undead.

Some of the more recent editions have done some cool things like adding Jonathan and Mina Harker, which I like, but also some other things that I haven’t liked as much such as replacing the goofy but simple and fun combat system. Other attempts have been made to balance out the Asshole Dracula Paradox, but in doing so some of the purity and directness of the mid-80s design has been lost. This is a game best experienced with the classic GW style, which pretty much never gave a shite, as they might say, about balance and predictability.

Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Supermajor season has officially kicked off, with the 2026 LGT entered into the books. Thoughts

Robots vs. zombies for our first Showdown of the week, pitting a different (and sadly fleeting) spin on Kastelans and Lords against the current Death Guard hotness. The Death Guard are looking to use a wall of Poxwalkers to hold fast while their Defilers do their work, with Mortarion to swoop in and clear out anything especially threatening. The AdMech have a surprisingly similar plan, aiming to grind the foe out with the Rad-Zone detachment rule, Skitarii and the tanks, with Characters and Kastelans to deploy to handle threats. Less pure chaff, but an overlapping ethos.

Who comes out on top? I think the Death Guard have some challenges here. Their biggest one is that they really want two of their Contagions active, but are going to have to pick one and go with it. If they don't pick the boosted AP, they're going to really struggle to put the robots down, as Scriptural Prognosis is exceptional for no-selling a Defiler unless they get very lucky with Devastating Wounds. However, without the Stealth/-1 to hit, AdMech might just be able to cleanly wipe them off the table, especially as that Vanguard/Marshal/Manipulus unit out of a Dunerider threatens to cleanly lift the big Poxwalker unit. This being a game of Actions also makes the AdMech's detachment rule really shine, as unless the foe pushes forward (into the jaws of guns/robots) they could have their plans disrupted by a badly timed Battle-shock. Between a Callidus and good Battleline, the AdMech are also better set up to force Actions through when needed. Finally - the Robots actually can just one-punch Mortarion, if Cawl's got him Oathed. Not a sure thing, but within the bounds of possibility, so has to be accounted for.

What's the plan from the Death Guard's side? Perhaps be a bit less pushy with the Poxwalkers than normal - use one unit to block the AdMech from double tapping Sabotage turn one, but otherwise get them out of the deployment zone (no Radial Suffusion, mercifully), but don't just throw them away, and stage for pushing up with critical mass in the mid-game, ideally with the Defilers in tow. The AdMech aren't that great at being super proactive, so if you can keep them from scoring early, then try to grind them mid-late, that could plausibly work, though there is a risk that their better options for forcing scoring will prove a problem. Whether that or just a battle-shock riot, the AdMech did comfortably take the day.

title: One of Warhammer's best ex designers just released a free wargame, and it's basically Mordheim 2.0
content:
Fans of Mordheim, Frostgrave, and Trench Crusade, all need to look at Black Death City immediately. This free skirmish wargame is the first independent project from Sam Pearson, a former game developer at Games Workshop who lead design on both editions of Warcry and the excellent Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Spearhead, some of the most fun fantasy games to emerge from the Warhammer studio in the last decade.

Set in a fantasy city overrun by plague, in Black Death City players control warbands of mercenaries, cultists, or similar ne'er do wells, battling one another in the streets and ruins to claim treasure, territory, and glory. If that sounds like classic Warhammer spin-off Mordheim, that's because hell yeah this is like Mordheim.

Had anyone else written this game I might call it "a love letter to Mordheim", but considering Pearson's pedigree, I think it might actually be "the Mordheim remake Games Workshop somehow didn't make". For long-time Mordheim fans, I can give you a pretty good sense of the game just by describing the key differences:

  • Players alternate activating one model at a time, rather than moving their whole warband. Outnumbered warbands can activate their models a second time with "surge" activations, which give one instead of two actions.
  • Most model stats are the same, but there are no Strength, Toughness, or Attacks values; more durable foes are represented with a higher Life total, more deadly weapons with higher Attacks, Damage, and Critical Damage numbers.
  • When a model is wounded, there's no rolling to see if it's taken down, stunned, or out of action; instead, models on a single life point are 'bloodied', reduced to one action when they activate.
  • Hand to hand combat is more interactive. Both players roll attack dice for their weapons; starting with the fighter who charged or won an initiative roll-off, players select whether to spend their hits on dealing damage, or attempting to parry the opponent's hit.

Rules wise, two really key features of Mordheim return. Models can take an action to hide behind terrain, ducking down and becoming invisible to models without a clear line of sight until their next turn (or they run out into the open). And as well as rules for climbing from terrain and jumping across gaps, models that are injured while standing on a raised surface need to make an initiative test or fall off, possibly taking fall damage. I mentally insert a Wilhelm scream in any game where this occurs.

The four warbands in the rulebook so far are conspicuously Mordheimy, albeit with some twists; the Guild Mercenaries, Verminkin, and Death Covens will be very familiar to old heads, while The Blighted Cloister actually looks like it's based on the villains from the Warhammer Quest: Darkwater box set.

Pearson has lavished attention onto the warbands. They can each choose from several unique origins that alter the force composition rules and provide a distinctive stronghold to operate from, have two spell lists, unique skills, unique equipment, and really expansive rosters of troops to recruit from.

What's missing at the moment - and it's a big omission - is the campaign system. Pearson says it's coming. This is entirely a solo project, right down to the art which he's drawing himself, and at the time of writing his priority is finding all the inevitable typos in the 134 page rulebook. If you want to get involved, you can download the free rules and sign up for updates on the Black Death City website, and there's already a community for the game on Discord.

Person worked at the Warhammer studio from 2017 to 2025, initially as a game developer, before becoming the Product Development Manager for Warhammer 40k. He launched his YouTube channel shortly after leaving the studio - it's a great resource for insight into game development and game design challenges - and announced his intention to make his own game. I've been eagerly awaiting the results, and I'm hoping to get it to the table soon enough! I'll be sharing my thoughts in the Wargamer Discord Community as I test it.

If you like the idea of "Mordheim meets Warcry", you should also check out the Wyrdcry project, which is still going strong.

title: Lord of the Rings: The King's Gambit is a "beefier" board game than the beloved Star Wars original
content:
The Lord of the Rings: The King's Gambit, a new board game set in Middle-earth, launched on Kickstarter today. Well, I say 'new'. It's a reimplementation of The Queen's Gambit, a well-loved thematic Star Wars game from the 2000s. This new version promises the same cinematic gameplay, but co-designer Justin Jacobson tells me to expect a far "beefier", better-balanced experience.

Jacobson, along with Restoration Games co-founder and lead designer Rob Daviau, is revamping an epic, multi-platform strategy battle. One to four players play as either the Shadow or the Free Peoples, aiming to win the trilogy's historic war. You'll need to juggle the battle on Pelennor Fields, as well as a siege on Minas Tirith.

Success on either of these two battlefields could net you victory, but keep an eye on the board's third portion: Mount Doom. Here, Frodo battles his own willpower to try and cast the Ring into the volcano - and whether he does also determines the game's winner.

Restoration Games' crowdfunder, running from September 29 to October 20, is for two different deluxe versions of a game that'll later come to retail. One costs $199, while another 'Mithril Edition' sells for $499. Both use armies of minis and 3D, multi-layer boards to up the glamour.

So, why should you back it now? I asked Jacobson about the game's different iterations, as well as the exciting quirks of the new design:

Wargamer: What are the major differences between this and The Queen's Gambit?

Justin Jacobson: The biggest thing was to make the decision space a little more interesting and a little beefier for modern hobby gamers.

The original game had action cards with two actions on each card. You program your cards for the round, and then on your turn, you flip up the next card in your row and decide which action to take. That in itself is a very clever system, because you might plan on doing one thing, then by the time your turn comes, the state of the game has changed so much you change your mind.

So, one of the cool things we added is called Resolve. Each action has a little icon that looks like algebra: 'activate X squads', right? You have Resolve tiles for the round (two 'one's and two 'two's), and when you decide your action, you also decide which Resolve token to use. It might not seem like much, but two is double one, so it can become quite a powerful decision.

Another thing in the original game was bonus cards for meeting certain goals. Basically, you'd end up playing six cards in the row and having a very powerful moment, but it wasn't great for the other player sitting and watching you take a bunch of turns in a row.

We now have formal objectives you get at the start of the game. There's 10 of them, but you're only choosing five, so it might give different direction from game to game.

One of the main rewards of these cards is Momentum. Momentum lets you add an additional 'one' to your Resolve value. You can now go up to a maximum of four - and 'activate one Orc squad' versus 'activate four Orc squads' is a massive difference. Now you've got to decide when to spend that Momentum and what on. That change just made the game so much more strategically robust. I think hobby gamers are going to really enjoy that.

WG: How differently do the Free Peoples and the Shadow play?

JJ: Another thing we wanted to do was increase the game's asymmetry. There's some in the original game, but we wanted to highlight it. One of the main changes is that each side now has two win conditions rather than one: a military victory and a ring victory.

The Shadow forces are trying to overrun Minas Tirith, so their military victory requires them to have a majority of miniatures in the top level of Minas Tirith. This was the Queen's Room in the original game, so it's the most analogous victory condition to the original game.

On the other side, the Free Peoples are trying to stop the horde that's assaulting them. There are three Orc encampments on the Pelennor Fields map, and the Free Peoples win a military victory if they defeat all of them.

These two parts happen on different battlefields. And they say the best defense is a good offense, so if somebody's pressing you in Minas Tirith, you can put pressure on them on the Pelennor Fields to take their foot off the gas.

Then, there's the opportunity for a ring victory. On a separate Mordor board, Frodo and Samwise are trying to get the ring to Mount Doom by travelling across various spaces. They have a Will track, and you'll pull tokens from a bag to see how their will gets reduced as the journey gets more arduous. There's also a really cool Gollum track to show which personality is in control - making the path easier or harder.

The Free Peoples win if they get to Mount Doom and survive, and the Shadow wins if Frodo's will hits zero. What's interesting about it is it's not a direct battlefield like the others are. You have control over the battlefields, but you have influence over Mordor. The main way you do that is objectives. As well as Momentum, a lot of these cards put good tokens into the bag for the Free People - or bad ones for The Shadow.

WG: What aspect of the design excites you the most?

The game still surprises me. I was at a mini con last week, and I demo'd the game about 10 times, and I saw two or three things I'd never seen happen before. One of the Shadow players had literally all of their Corsair forces in Minas Tirith. I had a game where it came down to the last bag pull, and Frodo had one Will left, and he couldn't pull a token that could save him.

It creates some really exciting moments. That diversity of game states will make it a really rich experience. That gives it a lot of legs. People will keep wanting to come back, because every game feels different.

WG: What do you get from the Kickstarter that you can't get at retail?

Importantly, the gameplay is the same between all three editions, including the retail edition Space Cowboys is putting out next year.

The Limited and Mithril Editions basically come with a second box to give it more of an epic feel. That includes a 3D Minis Tirith and Mount Doom that are only in the limited editions. The boards are also a little bigger in these editions.

Plus, each class of miniature has a different color plastic in the Limited Edition, while the retail edition just has two different colors. The Mithril Edition also has all sorts of bonus miniatures.

For example, there's a really cool hidden Eowyn mechanic, similar to the hidden queen in the original game. Eowyn is disguised as a regular Rohirrim rider at the beginning of the game, and you can reveal her to do a bunch of damage to the Witch King. We give you an extra Eowyn miniature so you can swap her in.

The Mithril Edition includes upgraded card racks, a little tea light that glows inside Mount Doo, card sleeves, dice trays, and more. We didn't want to have stretch goals in this campaign, so everything we could think to include made it into its own edition. It makes it easier to reduce shipping and make sure everything arrives in good condition. All you need to decide is if you want to add a big neoprene mat that comes separately.

You can learn more about the game on the Kickstarter page. Want to learn more about this year's best board games? Check out our dedicated guide, or join the Wargamer Discord to keep up with all our latest stories.

title: [40K] The September 2026 Balance Updates: Overview
content:
The September Balance Update arrives, bringing us the last of three promised monthly updates, and setting the stage for the next three months of 40k. It includes big changes for various loyalist and traitor Marine factions, and also the regular round of updates for everyone else. This article provides an overview of the update.

Third time's the charm, as the saying goes. It's time for another balance update, this one the last of the three that have been scheduled monthly to ensure 11th Edition gets a healthy start in the world. This means that after this, we're locked in on the current rules (excepting new books) for the next three months, covering many of the biggest event's of the year, and the World Championships. It's a big one, both in impact and importance, so let's take a look.

The Review

As always, we've split this across separate articles for the game's superfactions, which you can check out below:

  • Chaos
  • Imperium
  • Xenos

No article for Loyalist Space Marines this time around, as they aren't changed (as far as we know) from their Codex (which you can see our coverage of here).

For more traitorous or esoteric Marines, however, this update has more to offer, and we have even more articles for you. The biggest change in this update is that all Marine factions get the new T5 and S5 profiles, and this also extends to Custodes bolt weaponry. You can find detailed writeups for these factions below:

  • Chaos Space Marines
  • Death Guard
  • Emperor's Children
  • Thousand Sons
  • World Eaters
  • Grey Knights
  • Adeptus Custodes

The Video

Campbell's done a video version looking at the changes if you prefer your article to be moving, with sound.

The Headlines

What's the hot scoop then?

All Marines Get the New Profiles

Seven of the game's factions get changes reflecting the new normal for Space Marines. This has...mixed results. Some of them do very well, others probably pay a little much for the boosts, and find themselves a little threadbare on the table. We've covered this in detail in the individual pieces above, especially for Chaos where the biggest changes happen.

This obviously does have an impact on the wider game too, and the key thing is that anything that's S/T4 is now meaningfully worse, and S/T5 matters less than it used to. It has the weird side effect that there really aren't any "T4 factions" left in the game now, which throws off all kinds of maths and assumptions about lethality.

3DP Detachments Get Multiple Dispositions

Following what we've seen for the new Marine and Ork Codexes, all Detachments that are 3DP now get to pick between two Dispositions rather than just one. This has widely varying impact - for some it's "huh, neat", some get offered Disruption and wonder if they're a joke to you, and others are rubbing their hands (or in the case of Tyranids, claws) together in glee. In general, this makes 3DP Detachments a better prospect, and it's a good change.

There are also some bigger swings on DP changes this time around, with a few long-time 3DP options going to 2DP, and our first 2DP 3-stratagem Detachments and 1DP 6-strats.

Orks Get Rebalanced Towards Melee

Ork shooting has landed very hot, probably too hot. The biggest offender (the already notorious Big Mek Dakkarig) gets some especially big point hikes, and in general the best shooting toys get toned down a bit.

Happily, it isn't just nerfs for the Orks. Where shooting has overperformed, traditional krumpin' with da personal touch has merely done OK, but not phenomenally, and lots of Ork melee units get a few points shaved off to make them a more appealing prospect.

Rules Changes

Wings: Now that these are in the App we don't get early sight of them. So - there probably are some, and I assume one of my esteemed colleagues will pick up the baton and edit them in here later on.

Overwatch No Longer Scores Critical Hits

TheChirurgeon: Hey it's the first of those changes we didn't get early access to. Now under Snap Shots is a new rider: The 6s you roll to hit on your Snap Shooting no longer count as critical hits, meaning they won't trigger [LETHAL HITS] or [SUSTAINED HITS]. That's a massive change, and leaves us honestly wondering what the hell they think Overwatch is supposed to do now - it seems like it's purely something you'll either hope to get off a single lucky hit with, or only for units with [TORRENT] weapons.

This is a massive blow to factions which rely on a large volume of non-Torrent firepower with Lethal Hits and/or Sustained, and by my reckoning primarily hurts the Astra Militarum (where Combined Arms gives LETHAL HITS to all of your units against certain targets), Chaos Space Marines (who can get either ability whenever they shoot), Emperor's Children Defilers, and Orks (Flash Gitz seem a lot less scary now).

The Impact

Wings: I'll say that this is a bold update to throw out just before the biggest gap we've yet had in 11th, but there's certainly tonnes to work with here. A lot of factions get pretty sensible changes, often just a small but very meaningful tweak, and a lot of these feel very well-considered. I worry a little about Death Guard and AdMech getting some aggressive buffs, since both have been on the upswing in the recent past, but for AdMech at least it's mitigated by Lords of the Forge going on the 2DP naughty step (though don't worry robot fans, Cohort goes down to 1DP so you can still combo with that). I do, however, like the Ork changes a lot - feels like a much better nuanced set of changes than the knee jerks we've sometimes had in the past, so good job there.

I think the only serious concern I have is around Grey Knights and Thousand Sons, who both have a very rough time on it. Both pay a premium for their updates, and neither really had the unit count to absorb it, nor benefits enough to justify the cost. A bit of a shame, and if there are any fine tunings made in the shorter term, I'd guess these will be where (plus anything riotously broken coming out of Codex Marines).

I think the biggest upside here and a good thing to close on is the change to 3DP Detachments having two Disposition options. This is exactly what we want to see before going into a period of stability, because it really broadens what some factions can work with, and rescues a few fan-favourite options like Subterranean Assault from Disruption prison.

TheChirurgeon: There's simultaneously a lot going on here and not enough. They took some big swings with Detachments, finally giving us good Purge the Foe options again and making some surprising drops for a few 3 DP options, but at the same time a lot of these points updates feel either nonsensical or too slight. Moving a unit's cost by 5 points rarely matters unless it's part of a number of changes for very specific factions with small unit counts, i.e. Emperor's Children, and hits to Grey Knights just feel like kicking a faction when it's down. I think the Adeptus Mechanicus make out very well here and the point drops to Death Guard make me believe that they can absolutely make a come back now just on the sheer volume of units they can field. I think there are interesting builds with World Eaters now that they've fixed Berzerkers and changed Berzerker Warband, but I'm less convinced they'll be good after the point increases to Terminators.

The big losers here are Grey Knights and Thousand Sons, who both eat shit this time around with big point increases to key units and little else to show for it. I think the Emperor's Children hits also hurt more than they help, but it's a marginal loss for them and similarly I think Chaos Space Marines armies won't love this update either when they realize that Chosen and Warp Talons swinging at S5 just don't do what they need to against marines. The Ork changes feel less like a kick in the teeth or fiddling around in the margins and more like a measured response, which is good to see.

Make sure to check out the rest of our review of the update from the links at the top, and happy gaming!

title: [40K] The September 2026 Balance Updates: Thousand Sons
content:
The September Balance Update brings us a much bigger shakeup than usual, as alongside points and detachment changes for all factions, loyalist and traitor factions that field Marines have received updates to bring them in line with the new Codex Space Marine profiles. This article covers the Thousand Sons.

Codex: Space Marines made substantial changes to the Space Marine factions, updating statlines and weapon profiles to reflect the army becoming a more elite group of superhuman warriors. Rather than let the Chaos factions flounder this time around (remember when we had to live with 1-wound Marines in 9th edition for a year?), Games Workshop have released updates for each Chaos Marine faction, bringing many (but not all) of their profiles in line with those in the new Marines book.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of these rules. All rules and points are subject to change until published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Detachments Changes

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones
  • Grand Coven now lets you choose between Disruption or Priority Assets as Dispositions.
  • Hexwarp Thrallband lets you choose between Reconnaissance or Take and Hold.
  • Rubricae Phalanx lets you choose between Priority Assets or Take and Hold.

None of these are really what you want, and no one is going to take Disruption over Priority Assets in Grand Coven.

On top of this, there were two major changes to the Rubricae Phalanx Detachment, specifically to Stratagems:

  • Infernal Fusillade changed again, going from 2 CP to 1. It now merely gives the unit’s bolters the [PSYCHIC] ability and removes the change to the weapons’ Strength characteristic. That makes sense, given they’re now all S5 anyways. On the other hand, given how common Feel No Pains against Psychic attacks are becoming, this seems like it’s potentially a marginal benefit unless you’re facing -2 to your hit rolls.
  • Unwavering Phalanx also changed, now only giving incoming attacks -1 to wound if their S characteristic is greater than your T characteristic. This might have been a little more powerful with T5 Rubrics, but for the life of me I’m not sure why it changed given that it’s limited to only Rubric Marines and those are far from the backbone of the Rubricae Phalanx Detachment.

Points Changes

Every single change here is a points increase for the faction, and a number of them are completely nonsensical: I can’t remember the last time I saw Ahriman in a competitive list, so why did he go up 5 points? Most of these are 5-point increases, though they’re a bit higher on Rubrics and Scarabs, to the point that it’s going to cause problems for Thousand Sons players.

Increases

  • Ahriman +5 to 105
  • Exalted Sorcerer +5 to 100
  • Exalted Sorcerer on Disc of Tzeentch +5 to 100
  • Infernal Master +5 to 105
  • Rubric Marines +15/+20 for 5/10 models
  • Scarab Occult Terminators +20/+40 for your first/second units, +45/+65 for your third unit
  • Sorcerer +5 to 100
  • Sorcerer in Terminator Armour +10 to 110 for your first/second units, 120 for your third

Datasheets

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

The big changes here are to Toughness and weapon Strength. On the Toughness front, Terminator Sorcerers and Scarab Occult Terminators went up to T6. This is particularly great on them because of their -1 to be wounded ability, which is more or less always on with the unit. This makes them substantially more durable, as now s10 weapons will only wound them on rolls of a 4+. Meanwhile, Ahriman, Sorcerers, Infernal Masters, and Rubrics all went to T5 as expected.

Impact

This is a pretty back-breaking set of point increases for the faction - Thousand Sons players were already struggling to find room for all of their units, particularly against armies like Custodes. There are functionally two builds right now for Thousand Sons: Grand Coven and Rubricae Phalanx. Grand Coven lists lose about 40-45 points on this update with the increases to Rubrics and characters. That likely means losing a unit of Chaos Spawned or Enlightened - a big ask for an army running 11-12 drops.

On the other hand, Rubricae Phalanx lists get completely hosed here: Any list running two units of ten Scarabs is now a minimum of 100 points in the hole for just its two terminator units with attached characters, and likely 130 when you factor in Rubrics and their attached characters. The Detachment isn’t any more useful - Rubrics got tougher but lost some value via Stratagem, and Scarabs being S5 on their bolters means that Infernal Fusillade is still just a very situational Stratagem for a unit that largely depends on full re-rolls to hit and [LETHAL HITS] from its character. This also points to why this points increase feels like a lot for the unit - you’re already punching up effectively into big targets with AP-2 bolters, and going from S4 to S5 only matters into a small number of targets, name those with T5, T8, or T9, and in most cases you’d cover those with volume anyways.

Thousand Sons players will need to do some real work figuring out how to make the faction work; Scarabs have a ton of staying power and output but lack the kind of OC you really want to see on a Take and Hold unit, and the army just doesn’t really have the unit counts to make action economy on Priority Assets work as well as it does for some other armies; this is an army of glass cannon units that wants to murder you and control the table with flamers and psychic attacks. The increased strength on marine weapons is likely to make most of the toughness boosts feel like a wash, though S5 inferno bolters are definitely more interesting than they used to be.

Final Thoughts

This is more or less a nerf to the Thousand Sons faction, with point increases that aren’t really met by commensurate improvements in either durability or damage output. Scarabs already felt plenty tough and the number of S10 weapons wounding them on 2+ was pretty small. Likewise, your offensive output was largely based on either [ANTI-INFANTRY 4+] psychic attacks, high volumes of flamers re-rolling wound rolls, or high volumes of bolters re-rolling hit rolls with [LETHAL HITS], making S5 bolters a cute but marginal improvement. The case for taking inferno bolters over warpflamers is still unconvincing, especially given your ability to use the Twist of Fate ritual to just bump up the AP on those flamer attacks. I suspect the next few months aren’t going to be kind to Thousand Sons players.
