title: [40K] The September 2026 Balance Updates: Chaos
content:
The September Balance Update arrives, bringing us the last of three promised monthly updates, and setting the stage for the next three months of 40k. It includes big changes for various loyalist and traitor Marine factions, and also the regular round of updates for everyone else. This article covers the Imperium factions.

As always, this is a big multi-part review, so you can check out the other parts below:

  • Overview
  • Imperium
  • Xenos

No article for Space Marines this time around, as they aren't changed from their Codex (which you can see our coverage of here).

You may also note that this particular article is a lot shorter than normal, and that's because each of the five traitor Astartes factions get their own dedicated article because of the size of the changes, which you can check out below:

  • Chaos Space Marines
  • Death Guard
  • Emperor's Children
  • Thousand Sons
  • World Eaters

This also means we have a rules review of Chaos factions that doesn't have Rob's name on it. Truly an augur of the end times, and definitely not because he wrote all the others linked above.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of these rules. All rules and points are subject to change until published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Chaos Daemons

Chaos Daemons have done surprisingly well in 11th edition so far, ranking among the game's top three factions, with multiple powerful builds to choose from. The key builds right now tend to fall into one of three categories: Blood Legion + Cavalcade running a ton of Bloodcrushers, Plague Legion Battleshock nightmares, and Legion of Excess + Warptide lists running lots of Fiends.

Detachment Changes

  • None

Points Changes

  • Bloodcrushers - 6 model units +10 points
  • Fiends - 3rd unit costs +10 points
  • Flesh Hounds - 5 model units +5 points
  • Skarbrand - +15 points

Rules Changes

  • Cavalcade of Chaos - From Beyond the Veil stratagem changed to cost 2CP.
  • Legion of Excess - Sensory Excruciation stratagem, designer’s note cleaned up to match the correct army rule. No actual change.
  • Legion of Excess - Thieves of Pain stratagem changed entirely. Now the stratagem can give a non Monster/Vehicle Slaanesh unit -1 to wound if Strength is higher than your Toughness for the phase, in either the opponents shooting phase or fight phase.

Impact

Loser

Thoughts

Shane: A few points nerfs here and there, but a semi large nerf to the Bloodcrusher/Mounted daemons build and Legion of Excess. The Cavalcade strat changing to 2CP does prevent top of turn 1 Rapid Ingress style play, but you can still do it if you go first. It costing extra does make it stress your CP usage a little more.

The big change is the Legion of Excess strat, not being able to move damage around to another unit (that probably gets FnP vs that damage) is pretty big. Effectively this strat changes so much that it requires a gameplay style change from the Legion of Excess player.

Chaos Knights

Chaos Knights have been struggling since the launch of 11th. Their army rule became redundant and the Despoiler, which was carrying the faction on its back, saw a massive increase in points. Since then we’ve seen a raft of points drops as well as datasheet changes to the army’s worst performing knights. All of that hasn’t really moved the needle, with the exception of the ability to take both war dog Detachments at the same time which has seen some marginal success, and with September being the end of monthly updates, CK players better settle in.

Detachment Changes

  • Infernal Lance - Can now take Purge the Foe as an option in addition to Priority Assets.

Points Changes

  • Abominant, Desecrator, Rampager: -5 Points to 350 (wow, you shouldn’t have)
  • Tyrant: -10 to 390
  • Ruinator: -15 to 325

Rules Changes

None

Impact

Winner

Thoughts

The Ruinator has moved from once being the most expensive Abhorrent frame Knight when the Codex initially launched to the cheapest Knight we’ve ever seen, and that’s after the changes to its datasheet. Does that mean you take it now? Honestly I’m not sure. It's a solid buff piece to the War Dog list, but it means you’re taking fewer trade pieces which the list depends on. There might be a Lords of Dread list that takes them, but the Knight is still really really bad.

On the brighter side, Infernal got Purge the Foe back which is absolutely the disposition that Detachment wants to be doing. That combined with the softening of the nerf that Despoilers received last patch may let that Detachment breathe again. That said, there may just be a 1 big plus many dogs Purge the Foe list in Infernal that can do some great things.

Wrap Up

That wraps up our look at the non-marine Chaos factions but if you want deeper dives into the traitor legions and their codex-blessed ilk, be sure to check out our full reviews for each faction separately. There's a ton to cover with this update so check out the links at the top, and happy gaming!

title: [40K] The September 2026 Balance Updates: Grey Knights
content:
The September Balance Update brings us a much bigger shakeup than usual, as alongside points and detachment changes for all factions, loyalist and traitor factions that field Marines have received updates to bring them in line with the new Codex Space Marine profiles. This article covers Grey Knights

Marines everywhere are getting tougher and more deadly, and that includes the shiniest, most secretive of the Space Marines. Storm bolters are being brandished menacingly at the rest of the galaxy, but will they have the desired effect? Let’s have a look.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of these rules. All rules and points are subject to change until published on the Warhammer 40K App.

TheChirurgeon: The Grey Knights remain the odd men out when it comes to being Space Marines: Although technically just as Marine-line and beefy as their Codex-compliant cousins, the Grey Knights never received a Primaris update, and tend to live as their own, separate faction. They rely more heavily on psychic powers and abilities, which makes them as a faction more akin to loyalist Thousand Sons than psychic Marines.

That said, their tricks are nowhere near as good as those of the Thousand Sons: Although more mobile, they lack the raw damage output their traitor counterparts can put up, and lack the kind of cheap bodies you'd want for this type of army to hold objectives or do actions (i.e. they have no Tzaangors). They're currently among the game's bottom third in terms of competitive play, and successful competitive lists tend to run the Warpbane Task Force.

Detachment Changes

  • Warpbane Task Force gains access to Purge the Foe.

Points Changes

Increases

  • Brother-Captain +5pts
  • Brotherhood Champion +5pts
  • Brotherhood Chaplain +5pts
  • Brotherhood Librarian +5pts
  • Brotherhood Techmarine +5pts
  • Brotherhood Terminators +10/10/15/20pts
  • Castellan Crowe +5pts
  • Grand Master +5pts
  • Grand Master in Nemesis Dreadknight +10pts
  • Grand Master Voldus +5pts
  • Interceptors +10/20pts
  • Nemesis Dreadknight +10pts
  • Paladins +15/15/25/30pts
  • Purgation Squad +10/20pts
  • Purifier Squad +15/30pts
  • Strike Squad +10/20pts
  • Stormravens now pay 10pts for a Hurricane Bolter.

Datasheets

  • All Terminators go to T6
  • All regular Infantry go to T5
  • Nemesis Dreadknights go to T9
  • Storm bolters and combi-weapons go to S5 AP-1
  • Hurricane bolters go to S5 AP-1 on the Stormraven, not the Land Raider Crusader. Probably an oversight, but don’t rule out that going up in points if/when that’s fixed.
  • Basic close combat weapons go to S5
Grey Knight - Justicar
Credit: Pendulin

Impact

Wings: This is a tricky one because Grey Knights benefit unusually broadly from the Marine updates, but boy are they not in a position where they can afford to be losing whole units from their lists. The upside for them is that they pack a lot of (now much better) storm bolters, and can actually expect these to do some damage now rather than being incidental. Unfortunately it comes at a price of essentially a minimum +10pts per MSU army-wide, and more on some big hitters like Paladins and Purifiers, which I just don’t think the army can absorb. Extra T doesn’t massively change what kills them, and although it’s neat that they remembered to give that to Dreadknights, 8 > 9 isn’t a big break point, and the new Marine book handing out a bunch of S10 weapons doing d3+3 damage compounds that. If it wasn’t already clear, I think Grey Knights are Losers here, these changes could definitely have been softer, and I don’t think the Characters needed changing at all.

TheChirurgeon: On the Detachment side I think it's good news for the Grey Knights to have Purge the Foe and Take and Hold as options for Warpbane Task Force. The Grey Knights are an army that would rather move around and kill things than sit on objectives all game, even if they have really strong OC. Having access to Purge gives them a new playstyle to explore, one where they can reliably drop in on opponents who'd otherwise want to hide while using OC 3 terminators to prevent scoring against Priority Assets.

Wings: If there's any good news, it's that the new storm bolters work especially well with Brotherhood Strike, so you could see some more play from that detachment. Ultimately, however, I think there needed to be a cold hard look at just how sparse Grey Knight lists were already before.

Wrap Up

Wings: It does, at this point, feel like the 40k studio don't really know what to do with Grey Knights, and I hope they're fairly high on the Codex list - they're a faction that's very much in the waiting room for a do-over with the new Psyker rules. title: Wizards of the Coast lays off key community and social media managers for MTG and D&D
content:
Wizards of the Coast is going through another organizational restructure, and people have found themselves redundant. This time, it seems to be the community management and marketing team that's been hit. On Monday, LaTia Jacquise, community manager for Dungeons and Dragons, and Jordan Hopkins, social media manager for Magic the Gathering, announced that they had been laid off, something that Hopkins says was "part of a greater restructure".

Wargamer has reached out to Wizards of the Coast for comment, but at the time we published this article we hadn't received a response. We'll update you as soon as we hear anything from the team there.

Jacquise is a prominent figure in the D&D community and in the industry, first working for WotC in 2020 as the Adventurers' League Community Manager, before spending two years as the Community Relations Coordinator with Monte Cook Games. She rejoined WotC as the full time Community Manager for Dungeons and Dragons in November 2022.

This meant that her first big job was handling the catastrophic public relations fallout from the OGL disaster, a real baptism of fire. She has a wider creative career, including as a game designer, which you can find at her personal website.

Hopkins joined WotC as Social Media Marketing Manager for Magic the Gathering in August 2022, coming from a similar role at online card retailer Card Kingdom. If you've seen any official MtG social media content connected to the last four years of MtG sets, Hopkins was directly or indirectly involved. Hopkins is also a Twitch partner streamer, going by RayFK, and a participant with Loading Ready Run's annual Desert Bus charity marathon.

Writing on her LinkedIn account, Jacquise says "I have a lot of feelings that I'll probably never put words to, except to say that I don't regret a single day there and I have so much love for anyone else affected and for those who remain". Writing on his LinkedIn, Hopkins says "I obviously have many feelings about this, but I am still so proud of my work on the incredible show that is MagicCon and Magic: The Gathering FINAL FANTASY".

These experienced marketers state that they're considering their next moves and looking for more work. If you happen to be a geek industry insider with a vacancy, why not reach out to them? And consider coming to hang out in the Wargamer Discord community - it's the kind of place you'll enjoy.

title: The new Call of Cthulhu strategy board game stars the old gods "at the height of their power"
content:
As far back as Risk, board games have seen players wage war for control of planet earth, and Twilight Imperium and many games like it have expanded the scope out into a war for the galaxy galaxy. Call of Cthulhu: Old Ones Origins is set to outdo them all, in narrative scope at least: when I interviewed game designer Samuel Bailey, he explained this Lovecraftian strategy game is set "at the dawn of creation… where the ancient old ones are fighting for control of the universe and all that comes after".

Old Ones Origins is the newest project from Call of Cthulhu publisher Chaosium. It's a reimplementation and evolution of the rules from Warhammer 40,000: Forbidden Stars, which Bailey co-designed with James Kniffen at Fantasy Flight Games - a game I fought to get on Wargamer's guide to the best board games when it covered all-time greats instead of contemporary titles, I fought for it to have a place. Big and bombastic though the Warhammer 40k universe is, Bailey says that his new game is even more audacious.

The game is set "before there were even the laws of reality", with up to four players each playing the role of one of the Great Old Ones "at the height of their power". "This isn't old sleepy Cthulhu that's been slumbering under the ocean for countless millennia", Bailey says, "this is him as an awesome god of war and chaos". Hastur isn't "a failed emperor, he's at the height of his decadent imperial power, controlling and manipulating people".

And Yog Sothoth? "I mean, Yog Sothoth is exactly the same because he's beyond time and space, so he's unchanging in that regard". Of course.

This is an era that Lovecraft's stories imply, and which the wider Mythos built by August Derleth and generations of nerds have formalized: the first age of the universe, when the Great Old Ones were the Great Young Ones, and their full power was unleashed on a nascent Galaxy. It's a different angle on cosmic horror. "You're destroying planets and blowing stuff up and using people as pawns, and to the Old Ones, it's just moving pieces around the board". it's slightly meta

Old Ones Origins is a wargame, with players competing to lock down this nascent reality by applying arcane magical seals onto sections of the map to "seal away that part of the universe for yourself, following your rules and your power". These seals are the main tiebreaker if the war ends without an obvious winner - but if they're tied, "then Azathoth" - the blind idiot god, who dreams reality into existence - "wakes up, and reality ceases to exist".

I'm a big fan of the original Forbidden Stars, and while I was an easy mark for the Warhammer 40k theme, what made it mechanically compelling (and such a shame that planned expansions were never released) was the deeply asymmetrical playstyles between the factions. And you don't get much more asymmetrical than the Great Old Ones…

Cthulhu

Cthulhu may be the simplest of the Great Old Ones - his monsters are massive. "Even though this is before him being under the ocean, it still has that theme of him really toughing it out… being in a transient state and resurrecting". That is not dead which may eternal lie… Aside from spawning physically imposing Cthonians, a big mechanical focus for Cthulhu is 'fractures', a mechanic "representing reality tearing apart because these entities are battling and no one has control over it".

At the end of each conflict, "you add fractures for how many factions still have figures there at the end, up to a max of five" - an interesting admission, since the base game only ships with four factions. Then, when you start a conflict, "everyone takes psychic damage equal to the amount of fractures there". Cthulhu is particularly toxic to the fabric of reality, "getting bonuses for having fractures… able to spread them around or add them in certain places".

Not that Cthulhu's minions are immune to their ill effects. "You resist psychic damage with your unit's Power" - which, as in the Call of Cthulhu RPG, represents magical facility - "and his units don't have a huge amount". But there is an upgrade option for chaff cultist units, Graven Idols, which allows fractures to be harnessed into bonus magic.

Hastur

Hastur, the King in Yellow "focuses on having people bow to him by exhausting them, so he has a lot of mechanics that exhaust your enemies and yourself, and then gets bonuses on the amount of exhausted people that are around". 'People' is a word used advisedly in this case. Exhausted units can't defend themselves in a fight, so this has the potential to be devastating.

"He has a lot of tricky stuff, playing with resources, some more wild effects", Bailey adds. He gives the example of "one of his schemes, which I think is called the 'The Players Unmasked' - you just awaken everyone's avatar on one planet for a turn", inducing a spontaneous royal rumble between reality shattering godlings.

Other abilities are subtler. One forces "everyone with units in a region to exhaust one unit, but they get a resource for it". Hastur can target one of his own weak cultists as a way to get a little economic boost, or pick a location where their opponent only has a single powerful unit, giving them no choice but to knock over their big bruiser and open the way for an invasion. "It's a nice little troll faction for people who like that sort of thing", Bailey says.

Yog Sothoth

Yog Sothoth, as previously mentioned, exists outside time and space. "His main theme is breaking the rules… I don't need to move my guys, I'll just appear over here because what even is space?" One upgrade to the Pack of Tindalos - a variant name for the Hounds of Tindalos because, as the game is set before planet earth exists, neither do doggos - allows them to "pass through the rifts in time and space that normally block everybody". These changeable rifts separate areas of the map and can naturally fluctuate throughout the game, isolating and connecting areas unpredictably, so this ability gives incredible flexibility.

Combat between units is resolved partly with unit strength and dice rolls, and partly with combat cards. Yog Sothoth's magical nature means "his combat power comes less from his units and more from his spells and conflict cards". He has some particularly nasty tricks. Some parts of the board are 'nexus areas', where players can participate with their cards even if they have no units. Yog Sothoth's superior card power makes him very good at influencing these battles, and he has cards that can teleport his own troops in to claim victory from the exhausted forces of other Old Ones.

Shub Gorath

Shub Gorath, the Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young, "focuses on filling the board with as many units as possible". Their base unit is the Spawn, which are "zero statted units - no dice, no defense, no magic, but when you summon one, you get two of them". There's even an upgrade, "unending numbers, you can have any number of Spawn and effectively just fill the board with meat". They have no inherent defenses or offensive abilities, but there are ways to "give your spawn a defense, or a die, or a power for a round", and "they have a lot of conflict cards that get bonuses if you have more units than your opponent".

Bailey recalls one game "fighting Cthulhu, they were sitting on a planet with four fractures on it, and I invaded with like 12 Spawn, and immediately four of them just died because they're not rolling any dice, I have no way to block the the psychic damage from the fractures". But seven Spawn remaining was enough: "I still won that battle by playing cards and stuff that gave me bonuses". Cthulhu's Starspawn were dragged down by "a wave of flesh".

A Gamefound Campaign for Call of Cthulhu: Old Ones Origins is currently live on Gamefound, and is open until October 15. The standard edition of the game is going for $94, while a mini-heavy deluxe edition is $157 - plus shipping fees and tariffs.

As ever with crowdfunding campaigns, consider whether the discount on offer is enough to outweigh the wait for fulfilment and the uncertainty of crowdfunding. Chaosium's last crowdfunded boardgame, Horror on the Orient Express, is currently shipping its final pledge rewards to backers, two years and five months after the campaign closed.

I was excited for this game when I heard it was a remake of Forbidden Stars. Chatting to Bailey I found he was brimming with ideas to improve on that classic design, and a had creative flair for presenting the Lovecraftian cosmos in a genuinely fresh way. I'm hoping to get a demo game with him soon, and I'll share the results with you here, and in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: D&D teases a bizarre, Control style spin-off of a popular Ravenloft setting
content:
An unusual trailer has reared its head on the D&DBeyond website. Project_Lamordia appears to be a modern reimagining of one of Ravenloft's most popular Domains of Dread. Rather than your classic D&D fantasy, the trailer (see below) promises major Control vibes. Think labyrinthine labs and spooky cyberkinetic experiments gone wrong.

For the uninitiated, Lamordia is D&D's Frankenstein pastiche. It's a demiplane ruled by Viktra Mordenheim, a quirky scientist obsessed with the idea of eternal life. She found a way to bring her lover back from death, but forever changed into a construct with a serious identity complex. Project_Lamordia is still stuck in the mists of Ravenloft, but now it offers modern luxuries like computers and (presumably) killer robots.

It's not clear from the trailer what Project_Lamordia actually is. My best guess is a mini adventure, perhaps with a few new character options thrown in. There's a Redditor who claims to have seen an older version of the D&DBeyond page, and it apparently promised new backgrounds, and a level one-to-three adventure with pre-made adventurers. There's no way to verify if these claims are true, however.

All will, apparently, be revealed on October 13, the spookiest day of the year. If you want to kill time before then, check out the spookiest character options in our DnD races guide. Or hit us up in the Wargamer Discord - I will take literally any opportunity to talk about horror, Dungeons and Dragons, or both.

title: Can GW's new Warhammer scheme replace the beloved free mini of the month?
content:
Games Workshop has revealed the replacement for its popular mini-of-the-month scheme: in-store paint-and-take sessions led by staff, featuring a choice of eight free Warhammer 40k and Age of Sigmar miniatures. These sessions will be available in Warhammer stores from October 10, and the studio hasn't specified an end date for the scheme, suggesting it will join the regular rotation of in-store activities along with game nights.

The Warhammer 40k figures will be a Necron Warrior, Cadian Shock Trooper, Adepta Sororitas Battle Sister, or Chaos Space Marine Legionary; the Age of Sigmar minis are a Chaos Warrior, Deathrattle Skeleton, Orruk Gutripper, or Cities of Sigmar Steelhelm.

The Warhammer Community post announcing the new activity suggests it's a way to "try out a new colour scheme" and "call on the expertise of the store staff to get help with a new painting technique". The new initiative will also give early access to the exciting new Warhammer Tone Pro paints revealed during the Big Warhammer Autumn Preview.

This looks to be a similar activity to the "first one's free" Space Marine painting lesson GW offers for brand new customers, but aimed at slightly more enfranchised hobbyists. Maybe the goal is to encourage people to form or join the regulars who paint their minis (and spend their money) in the store.

Games Workshop HQ may not see this as a direct replacement for mini of the month, but as the new scheme launches the month after the old one ended, customers likely will. GW started offering one free miniature each month, no strings attached, in January 2021, as a way to coax wary customers back to Warhammer stores after COVID lockdowns. To incentivize spending, it offered monthly challenge coins for customers who spent at least $100 in one go.

Did it work as a promotion? That's between the Emperor and GW's accountants. Maybe the free selection of minis from diverse Warhammer 40k factions and AoS armies brought in new customers and encouraged them to spend directly in store - or maybe it just resulted in the same old customers getting freebies.

What was your experience of the mini of the month? Did it change how you approached the hobby, inspire you to pick up a new army, or drain your wallet? Or was it just a neat monthly freebie? Join the discussion in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Warhammer 40k Astra Militarum codex, lore, and new models
content:
The Warhammer 40k Astra Militarum army - a.k.a. the Imperial Guard - is among the oldest and most popular playable factions in Games Workshop's sci-fi wargame. An enormous force of trillions of regular humans, the Guard are humanity's first - and often only - line of defense. This complete guide includes full details of the most recent Astra Militarum codex including the killer Death Korps of Krieg models - so read on for everything you need to collect and play Imperial Guard in 10th Edition!

For an explanation of all the other armies fighting it out in GW's grimdark galaxy, read our full guide to the Warhammer 40k factions. And to find out which armies are getting new rules next, check our updated list of Warhammer 40k codex release dates.

Use the links below to jump to what you need - from the latest new models, to the lore and background of the Astra Militarum and the various Imperial Guard regiments, to our breakdown of the 10th edition codex (which remains in play at the launch of Warhammer 40k 11th Edition, remember). I've even added glamor shots of my own Astra Militarum regiment - the 728th Nassau Hoplites - to show that even averagely painted Guard models can look badass!

  • New releases
  • Lore
  • Codex and rules
  • Combat Patrol
  • Regiments

New Astra Militarum models in 2026

After a year or so out of the spotlight, Imperial Guard fans are now getting a bevy of gifts, because Games Workshop released five brand new Astra Militarum units in 2026, as part of 10th Edition's last hurrah: the Return of Yarrick narrative expansion.

  • Commissar Yarrick
  • Commissar Graves (on foot)
  • Commissar Graves (on Vigilance)
  • Centaur RSV
  • Hippogriff AFV

First off, we've got old Bale-Eye himself, Commissar Yarrick, back from the dead to lead Guard forces on Armageddon once again. But he's not the only unexpected Officio Prefectus reinforcements joining the war.

Commissar Graves (on foot)

Fearsome female commissar Thenia Graves is a new named character joining 40k in the Return of Yarrick storyline. We don't know much about her, except she can dual wield power fist and power sword (noyce) and, per WarCom, she's so obsessed with "ironclad discipline" she makes Yarrick look like the Good Cop. Yikes.

Commissar Graves (on Vigilance)

There's no doubting Commissar Graves is the new Billy Big Boots in Guard Town - because she comes with her own customised version of the new Centaur transport, named Vigilance. It's tripped out with everything an ostentatious Militarum leader needs: upgraded guns, lots of gold aquilas, a big regimental flag, and a heavy armored ram - because hanging out in the backlines is for cowards and heretics.

Centaur RSV

No, that's not a Bolt Action model; we're still in the 41st (or early 42nd) millennium, not World War Two. For reasons no doubt deliberately devised to have real world war historians grinding their teeth, the Guard are using half-tracks now - and we're 100% down with it. The Centaur RSV (Rapid Strike Vehicle) is a lighter, presumably faster alternative to the Chimera transport tank.

Hippogriff AFV

This isn't a WW2 miniature either, honest! The Hippogriff AFV (Armored Fighting Vehicle) is the Astra Militarum's first tabletop armored car, and appears to be a cheaper way to add mobile firepower to a mainly infantry based force.

With four primary weapon options (battle cannon, lascannon, onslaught gatling cannon, or melta cannon) and a choice of heavy stubber or meltagun as secondary, it's going to be a flexible little beast, too.

How on earth can you mount that big a cannon on a titchy little car? How the hell is it loading or ejecting shells? Don't ask questions. The Emperor Protects.

Who are the Astra Militarum?

In Warhammer 40k, the Astra Militarum (affectionately called 'The Guard') is the primary standing army of the Imperium of Man. It's composed of billions (possibly trillions) of unaugmented, ordinary human soldiers, drawn from planets all over the galaxy, and organised into millions of vast regiments.

Those countless human infantry soldiers are backed up by enormous numbers of tanks, support vehicles, and aircraft maintained by the Adeptus Mechanicus; supported by battlefield specialists including sanctioned psykers; and ferried to wars across the galaxy in the void-ships of the Imperial Navy.

The 'Guard' has existed, in various different structures and under different names, for over 10,000 years, since its original formation by the Emperor of Mankind in the late 30th Millennium to help fight his Great Crusade.

At that time it was called the Imperial Army (Imperialis Auxilia) - and would play a massive role in the many battles of the Horus Heresy civil war, with army regiments fighting alongside Space Marine legions on both the traitor and loyalist sides.

Of all the 40k armies to collect, play, and read books about, the Astra Militarum may be the most dearly beloved by fans. There are lots of reasons for that, but we reckon relatability is top of the list - these troopers are just regular old humans like you or I, and that means we can feel their pain, their fears, and their triumphs more keenly.

In the far future of the 41st millennium, the Emperor's domain is beset by dangers beyond comprehension, from nefarious Chaos Space Marines wreaking revenge on the empire that exiled them, to the encroaching alien menace of the Tyranid hive fleets - insectoid swarms bent on consuming the whole galaxy.

The Guard face all those terrifying foes with nothing but flimsy armor, low-power laser guns, old fashioned bayonets, and slow, clunky tanks slammed together on a budget - and they often win. That's a compelling theme for sci-fi wargamers.

Sure, the most famous defenders of humanity are the Space Marines, gene-crafted demigods who stand as a bulwark against the worst the universe has to throw at them. They're peerless in battle, but they're few, and can't win galactic wars on their own.

In their own way, the human soldiers of the Imperial Guard boast far more bravery, grit, and determination than even the Adeptus Astartes can muster.

Reasons to play Astra Militarum

The Astra Militarum are one of the 'classic' 40k armies, and there's no better time to collect and play them than now, with revamped models for not just the core Cadians, but specialist regiments and units like the Death Korps of Krieg, Rough Riders, and Ratling Snipers too.

But they're not without their drawbacks, and, like any 40k army, they won't suit everyone.

Play Astra Militarum if:

  • You enjoy a coordinated, multi-part strategy, and are comfortable with calculated losses.
  • You're more interested in shooting than melee assaults.
  • You like Big Guns And Tanks.

Don't play Astra Militarum if:

  • You aren't prepared to buy and paint a lot of models.
  • You aren't prepared to lose a lot of models every game.
  • You want to get into close combat - the Astra Militarum's very best melee units are really just there to counterpunch enemy assaulters, not to lead the charge.

Astra Militarum codex and rules for 11th edition

Games Workshop's latest Astra Militarum codex is the 10th Edition book, first released on its own on February 15, 2025. This remains valid into 11th Edition.

If you're new to 40k, this is the dedicated rulebook for the Astra Militarum army, which you'll need to play. Alongside some lore details, it contains your core army rule, all the datasheets which explain how your units, weapons, and abilities function in-game, and five distinct detachments you can build your army around.

Games Workshop has also released some additional free detachments which encourage different kinds of army building - you can find them in the downloadable faction pack on the Warhammer Community downloads page.

Army rule - Voice of Command

The Astra Militarum's core rule, Voice of Command, is all about using your army officers to yell Orders at the troops, giving the right bonuses to the right units, at the right times.

In the command phase at the beginning of each turn, each of your officers can issue one (or more) orders to a unit within six inches of them, and the target unit will get a specific benefit until the next command phase.

There are six orders available - here's what they do:

  1. Move! Move! Move! - Add 3 inches to target unit's move.
  2. Fix Bayonets! - Add 1 to target unit's Weapon Skill.
  3. Take Aim! - Add 1 to target unit's Ballistic Skill.
  4. First Rank, Fire! Second Rank, Fire! - Add 1 to Attacks for target unit's Rapid Fire weapons.
  5. Take Cover! - Improve target unit's save by one (max 3+).
  6. Duty and Honor! - Improve target unit's Leadership and Objective Control stats by 1.

Lower ranking officers can only issue one order per turn, but more powerful characters can hand out two or even three. Remember, though, that a unit can only be affected by one order at a time (unless some other ability lets them benefit from more).

Detachments

The 10th edition Imperial Guard codex has five detachments that -  unusually for an army with a reputation for only playing one way - genuinely offer distinctive ways to play and win games.

Each detachment has its own unique Detachment Rule which, together with the Army Rule, will define your core strategy by making you stronger in one particular area. Within each detachment, you also have a menu of four paid Enhancements to buff up your characters, and six custom Stratagems to activate for bonuses at crucial moments  during the game (at the cost of Command Points).

Here are the five detachments, with a breakdown of their key rule, and a summary of their best bits.

Combined Arms

Detachment Rule: Born Soldiers

  • Regiment units (most of your infantry) get the Lethal Hits ability when shooting non vehicle, non monster targets.
  • Squadron units (tanks and vehicles) get the Lethal Hits ability when shooting monster or vehicle targets.

Play Style

Balanced - Supports a mixture of infantry and vehicles, offense and defense.

Best Enhancement

Grand Strategist - given to an Officer model, allows them to issue one more order per turn

Best Stratagems

  • Reinforcements! (2CP) - After an Infantry Regiment unit dies, bring it back in Strategic Reserves at full strength
  • Flexible Command (2CP) - In the command phase, instead of the usual restriction to Regiment units, any number of officers can issue their orders to any units, including tanks.

Siege Regiment

Detachment Rule: Artillery Support

Each battle round, select one artillery barrage to fire:

  • Creeping Barrage - Roll a d6 for each enemy unit more than 12″ from your army. For every 5+, that unit is Shaken and takes -2 to move, advance, and charge rolls this battle round.
  • Incendiary Bombardment - Select 3 enemy units more than 12″ from your army. This battle round, those units are Scattered and cannot have the benefit of cover.
  • Smoke Shells - Select 3 friendly units. This battle round, those units have the Stealth ability (-1 to hit when shooting them).

Note: the second two options change to target only 2 units in smaller Incursion games, and 4 units in big Onslaught games.

Play style:

Massed infantry charge supported by artillery - the Death Korps of Krieg approach.

Best Enhancement:

Stalwart's Honors - given to an officer leading a unit, that unit gains the benefit of Take Cover! in addition to the benefit of any other order it's given.

Best Stratagems:

  • Callous Sacrifice (1CP)- Pick a Platoon unit in melee combat, and you can ignore the restriction on shooting the enemy units it's in combat with. But, every time you wound one of those enemy units this phase, roll 1d6 and your nominated unit loses a model for every 4+.
  • Over the Top (2CP) - one officer can issue the Move! Move! Move! order once to every eligible Infantry unit, regardless of range.

Mechanized Assault

Detachment Rule: Armored Fist

Add one to wound rolls when a unit shoots after disembarking from a transport.

Play style:

Aggressive, mobile infantry maneuvers using transports for board and objective control

Best Enhancement:

Bold Leadership - gives the bearer's unit (or any transport it's embarked in) 'sticky objectives' - objectives they capture remain in your control after you leave them, until the enemy takes them.

Best Stratagems:

  • Clear and Secure (1CP) - one infantry unit can re-roll all hits and wounds this shooting phase, providing it just disembarked from a transport.
  • Rapid Dispersal (1CP) - one infantry unit that just disembarked from a transport can immediately make a 6″ move.

Hammer of the Emperor

Detachment Rule: Iron Tread

All Squadron units (vehicles) automatically advance six inches instead of rolling, and can move through enemy units' engagement ranges (but not end moves there).

Play style:

TANKS!

Best Enhancement:

Calm Under Fire - Once per turn, when a vehicle officer (Tank Commander) issues an order to a Squadron unit, it can immediately issue the same order to another Squadron unit.

Best Stratagems:

  • Blazing Advance (1CP) - used on a Squadron unit that just advanced - it can still shoot despite advancing.
  • Furious Cannonade (1CP) - used on a Squadron unit in the shooting phase - Improve your ranged attack's AP by one if the target is within 12″.

Recon Element

Detachment Rule: Masters of Camouflage

Your Walker and Regiment units permanently have the benefit of cover - and when actually in cover, improve their save by another one (max 3+).

Play style:

High skill positioning gameplay, precision attacks, and deployment shenanigans to unbalance opponents.

Best Enhancement:

Tripwires - Each time an enemy unit ends a normal, advance, charge, or fall back move within 9″ of the bearer's unit, roll a d6. On a 4+ the enemy unit is stunned and gets -1 to all hit rolls until next turn.

Best Stratagems:

  • Draw them out (1CP) - One Platoon unit can make an immediate, reactive 6″ move when an enemy unit ends its normal, advance, or fall back move within 9″ of it.
  • Tanglefoot Grenades (1CP) - Used at the start of your opponent's charge phase on one friendly Grenades unit - until end of phase, all enemy charges against this unit take -2 to their charge roll.

As with all 10th edition detachments, each of these gameplay-distinctive ways to play the army is 'subfaction agnostic' - so it can be applied to any army list, regardless of which lore-appropriate (or home-brewed) regiment you want your Astra Militarum force to come from.

This is a departure from previous editions, where different rule sets within each faction were directly tied to officially mandated sub-factions like the Cadians, Catachans, or Armageddon Steel Legion. Some regiments from the lore do have specific units that lean more towards one detachment's strategy than others.

For example, the newly reinforced Death Korps of Krieg's Artillery Team has access to more powerful gunnery than the Cadians' Field Ordnance Battery, so might make for better fire support in a Siege Regiment army; that detachment is directly themed around GW's background fiction for the Krieg armies.

But it's all just down to personal preferences of theme and models. There are no formal restrictions on mixing Death Korps of Krieg, Cadian, and other models in your army, regardless of detachment choices - I'm thoroughly looking forward to welcoming Krieger reinforcements into my majority-Cadian force. 

Astra Militarum Combat Patrol

One of the prime benefits of an Astra Militarum force is the breadth of troops, models, and Imperial Guard tanks available to you. Whilst it's incredibly exciting to look at the variety you can choose from, it can also be a little overwhelming. Luckily, there's a definitive Warhammer 40k starter set for the army: the Astra Militarum Combat Patrol box.

Games Workshop brought out the most recent Combat Patrol box for the Guard in February 2025, featuring a frankly weird set of units, including some of its newer kits. It costs $170 / £100 direct from GW, but as usual you can find it for less at local game stores and via Amazon ($140 / £95).

The current Astra Militarum Combat Patrol box contains 25 miniatures, made up of these units:

  • Cadian Command Squad x 1 (five models)
  • Rough Rider x 10
  • Kasrkin x 10

As a force on its own, it plays an aggressive, high risk game. You'll need to lay down effective long range fire with your elite Kasrkin squad, supported with orders and buffs from the Command Squad - while you send the Rough Rider cavalry thundering up the board to take objectives and head off threats.

Played right, these units can kick out good damage every turn, with options for anti-tank weapons - but those vulnerable riders will die easily once they're in the thick of it, and you'll be lacking any cannon fodder or armored threats to divert enemy fire.

The box also lacks any reliable longer range, or indirect fire, guns to rain hell on the opposing force - a key Astra Militarum strength - and only has one Officer character to hand out orders, drastically limiting the effectiveness of your core army rule.

So: canny upgrades to the Combat Patrol army might be:

  • A Leman Russ battle tank - a cheap, tough, and fairly powerful gun platform to bully enemy lines and take heat off your Rough Riders.
  • A Field Ordnance Battery or Krieg Artillery Team - to add long range supporting firepower your opponent will have to deal with.
  • A second Officer, like a Cadian Castellan  - to double your orders.
  • Two squads of Cadian Shock Troops - basic infantry squads to push onto empty objectives and soak up fire if needed, keeping your more powerful Kasrkin alive longer to rack up kills.

Astra Militarum regiments

Throughout the Imperium, thousands of planets are compelled to form their own Imperial Guard regiments, conscripting many millions of troops in the name of the God Emperor. The Imperium is colossal beyond all imagination - so you can create your own Imperial Guard regiment, customising them to use the rules and paint schemes you prefer.

However, the setting features several 'official' Imperial Guard regiments that have become legends throughout the Imperium, and, as a result, have often had specific rules and histories in the game. Here are some of the most popular and famous regiments known to humanity - we'll start with the ruthless, gas-masked men and women of the hour…

Death Korps of Krieg

Of the many regiments, the intimidating Death Korps of Krieg are the one you'll see most of right now, as Games Workshop has just released a whole army set for them, with more brand new kits to come.

But just who are these grim-looking, trench-coated guys? In short, they're the most fatalistic, dogmatically loyal, and fearless warriors in the whole damn Guard - and that's because of their horrific, tragic backstory.

The planet of Krieg once suffered a civil war, with many trying to secede from the Imperium. After centuries of brutal trench warfare and atomic bombardment, the loyalists raised the Imperial aquila above a ruined world.

Today, in shame, the Death Korps of Krieg attempt to make up for this betrayal by fighting harder, suffering more, and pushing themselves past fear in service of the Imperium. Though the Krieg would never reject their duty, no matter how onerous, they have an unfounded reputation for seeking death. They know that their life belongs to the Emperor, and it is his to take when he wills it, not theirs to throw away.

Armageddon Steel Legion

The hive world of Armageddon is known for fending off a colossal horde of Orks on several separate occasions. As a result of the many invasions it's survived, the planet maintains a large Imperial Guard regiment, known as the Armageddon Steel Legion. They're a motorized infantry force, fielding many infantry squads in Chimaera transports, necessary for crossing the polluted wastes that cover much of Armageddon.

Cadian Shock Troopers

For millennia, the planet Cadia held vigil over the Eye of Terror, a hideous rent in space-time where reality overlapped with the raw stuff of Chaos. This proximity to humanity's most deadly enemies led the Cadian Shock Troopers to become one of the most famous and most numerous of all Astra Militarum regiments.

Alas, during Abaddon the Despoiler's 13th Black Crusade, Cadia was finally destroyed. The Cadians may have lost their home, but they have not lost their determination. As their last commander, Ursarkar E. Creed said, "The planet broke before the guard did". With untold millions of Cadians serving in wars across the galaxy, they fight on, taking the fight to Chaos wherever they can.

Catachan Jungle Fighters

This death world is a jungle paradise, until you set foot on it. Everything wants to kill you there, and we do mean absolutely everything. The Catachan Jungle Fighters make up the core of this Imperial Guard regiment, deadly foes who look down on anyone who hasn't suffered as they have.

The Catachan's have a reputation for strength and brutality, and have earned the nickname "little Ogryns" - but don't let them hear you say that. They don't take to Imperial discipline too kindly, and there is a particularly high rate of mysterious accidents among Commissars assigned to Catachan regiments.

Mordian Iron Guard

The Mordian Iron Guard Regiment hails from the tidally locked hive world of Mordian. One half of the planet is a scorching desert pointed constantly towards the system star, while all human settlement exists in hives on the frigid dark side. A sinister world, its regiments have a reputation for ruthless discipline and efficiency.

Mordian has resisted repeated Chaos incursions, and has a proud history of dispatching regiments to fight in the Emperor's wars throughout the galaxy. The planet itself is located in Segmentum Obscurus on the far side of the Great Rift, meaning it is isolated in Imperium Nihilus. While all Mordian soldiers expect to die in duty, they now face the disquieting uncertainty that their home world is inaccessible and, possibly, lost.

Tallarn Desert Raiders

During the dark time of the Horus Heresy the world Tallarn was ravaged by an unforeseen invasion of the Iron Warriors. They rendered the planet toxic to all life with a virus bombardment, before commencing a ground assault in armored vehicles in search of some inscrutable prize.

The tank war that followed was the largest in the history of the Imperium, and its aftermath shaped the face of Tallarn for millennia since. Talarn is a lifeless desert world beset by dust storms whose population live in underground bunkers. The Tallarn Desert Raiders are experts in both light infantry combat and armored warfare, often using nimble infantry forces to harass, ambush, reconnoiter, and undermine the enemy before committing a decisive armored assault to finish the foe.

Valhallan Ice Warriors

Valhalla was a verdant world when it was first settled by humankind, and quickly became a bastion of civilization, but a collision with an iron meteorite drove it out of its orbit, rendering it into a frigid land of ice and death. If this environmental catastrophe were not enough, it was followed immediately by an invasion from an Ork warfleet.

The people of Valhalla proved their resilience against two terrible foes, starvation and the greenskin horde. The Valhallan Ice Warriors are winter warriors without compare, adept at surviving privation like few other regiments.

Vostroyan Firstborn

An industrial world, Vostroya has close links to the Mechanicus and Mars in particular. Their weapons tend to be well-maintained, out-performing other Imperial Guard regiments under similar circumstances. Their guard regiment, the Vostroyan Firstborn, may seem proud and ostentatious, but it is also a cover for a deep cultural shame.

During the Horus Heresy Vostroya was a hub of materiel manufacture for the Imperium. When the call to to defend the throne world against Warmaster Horus was issued, Vostroya refused to raise regiments, claiming that its manpower would be better served producing weapons for the war effort. Ever since it has pledged the firstborn children of its noble households to His service, to make amends for their laxity in the Imperium's direst hour.

Tanith First and Only

The plucky heroes of Dan Abnett's famous (and utterly fantastic) Gaunt's Ghosts novel series, the men and women Tanith First Light Infantry regiment have become living legends among the Imperial Guard.

The densely wooded planet Tanith raised three small regiments - mustering only 6,000 or so soldiers combined, plus a minimal complement of vehicles and artillery - but a catastrophic chaos assault hit the planet on the very day those regiments were formed, wiping out its entire population and nearly half the newly enlisted guardsmen.

Around 3,500 Guard survivors fled the planet's destruction, reforming into a single regiment - the morbidly named Tanith First and Only - under the leadership of Colonel Commissar Ibram Gaunt. Their thrilling exploits thereafter form the basis of Abnett's 16-book series Gaunt's Ghosts - named for the regiment's even more morbid nickname, which plays on both the Tanith's talent for sneaky warfare, and their tragic backstory.

The Tanith are masters of stealth reconnaissance, carrying forward skills learnt as hunters and trackers in the vast, dark forests which once covered their home planet. During the course of their many perilous and heroic postings in the Sabbat Worlds Crusade against Chaos, the Tanith First has picked up reinforcements from several other forces, most notably a complement of hardy citizens of the planet Verghast, who'd fought alongside them in the defense of Vervunhive during the events of the novel Necropolis.

Savlar Chem-Dogs

Not all Astra Militarum regiments are shining paragons of honor, duty, and loyal sacrifice to the throne. As a galaxy-wide totalitarian power, the Imperium has millions of prisons bursting with scum and villainy. So, naturally, like the Soviet Red Army that inspired so much of its lore, the Guard has penal legions: massive regiments of conscripted convicts, dredged up from the very nastiest corners of an already horrible society.

Foremost among those weaponized dregs of humanity are the infamous Savlar Chem-Dogs. Their home planet, Savlar, is a lawless, poisonous hell hole - used by the Imperium as a giant mine to harvest toxic chemicals, and a dumping ground for vast shipments of criminals and captives, all under the supervision of merciless Adeptus Arbites guards.

Savlar's unbreathable, chem-choked atmosphere means its people permanently wear their distinctive rebreather masks - and the horrendous living conditions imposed on everyone unfortunate enough to live there have turned its population into ruthless, self serving cut-throats, capable of unspeakable brutality (but only if there's something in it for them).

Only the Imperium could look at such a place and think 'we should make them fight' - but it found a way. Savlar offered its prisoners a ticket off their prison planet, in exchange for almost certain death fighting in the absolute worst battlefields imaginable - and, crucially, license to loot and salvage anything they might find there.

And so the Chem-Dogs were born: an army of vicious, amoral scavengers, treated as completely expendable by their commanders, and deployed explicitly to do as much damage as possible, then die.

Elysian Drop Troops

It's well known that every human army in science fiction needs its own painfully cool, far future version of paratroopers. In the Astra Militarum, that role is filled by the rarely seen, fan favorite Elysian Drop Troop regiments.

Lightly armored and equipped with back mounted grav-chutes and lightweight Accatran-pattern lasguns, Elysian Drop Troops specialize in quick, overwhelming surprise attacks from the air, or stealthy aerial insertions by Valkyrie dropship, followed by guerrilla warfare campaigns. If you get strong vibes of US Airborne divisions striking behind German lines on D-Day in 1944, that's because you're supposed to!

Even though their homeworld of Elysia is right in the middle of the Imperium, in Armageddon's backyard, we don't see much of the Drop Troops in 40k lore. That's partly because, due to their expensive, specialist equipment and inherent lack of armored support, they're only deployed in quite specific engagements, and rarely in vast numbers.

But - as proven by Halo ODST and Helldivers 2 - nerds love sci-fi paratroopers, making the Elysian Drop Troops a firm favorite. And by "nerds", we mean us. We love 'em.

How to convert Astra Militarum models

Out of all the armies in Warhammer 40k, the Imperial Guard are maybe the best positioned for conversions; hell, even an Airfix kit can be easily taken apart and used for an upgrade or visual change for your army.

The Astra Militarum allows for a huge degree of customization, with many stunning armies being made up of innovative and creative Imperial Guard conversions. As the entire design behind the Astra Militarum takes inspiration from World War II and World War I armies, you can easily mix in third-party parts or models from ranges like Warlord Games' Bolt Action, or even Black Powder, to spice up your army's visual appeal.

At the very easiest level, you can very easily personalize tanks by modifying infantry models to ride along on their hulls - or cut the legs off officers and stick them in the cupola to become Tank Commanders, as I've done with a Militarum Tempestus Tempestor Prime and a Leman Russ in the photo below.

Many companies, such as Pig Iron Productions, Victoria Miniatures (whose Guard-flavored 'Scrapper's Bag of Bits' product image you see above), or Anvil Industry also make troops that combine history with science fiction, making their models and conversion bits ideal for your Imperial Guard Conversions. Some companies offer a wider range of female model options, such as the excellent Bad Squiddo Games.

For plastic sci-fi regiments, you've got a few options. Wargames Atlantic produce several ranges - their own extremely varied Death Fields, and the Iron Core and SpaceNam kits made in partnership with other designers. Mantic Games have a great range of infantry and vehicles in the GCPS line. And then there's Warlord Games' Konflikt '47, which - while mostly metal and resin - has a growing plastic line focused on World War 2 superscience.

And that's all you need to know about the Emperor's loyal Astra Militarum for now! If you're a proud member of the Guard, why not join us in the Wargamer Discord community? For a round up of the best new stories on Wargamer every week, make sure you sign up to our newsletter.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.
